If we consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$ as a transformation from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m,$ then there are four fundamental subspaces of $A{:}$

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with dimensions $r$ and $m-r,$ respectively.

- $\text{Col}(A^T)$ and $\text{Null}(A)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with dimensions $r$ and $n-r,$ respectively.

Furthermore,

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ and

- $\text{Null}(A)$ and $\text{Col}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^n.$

Finally, we have that

- the image of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ and

- the image of $\text{Col}(A)$ under the action of $A^T$ is $\text{Col}(A^T).$

These facts about the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](images/37/37f633d0bca1a599f7d1658c051f802da5d607d420beeb4bddbef5cd98c366ef.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "190e1777-4f27-5c94-88bd-21c9992eb024" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5456 :tutorial/title "The Big Picture of the Four Fundamental Subspaces"} :step/id #uuid "8eef352e-273a-5614-b97d-8c357807e9a0" :step/math-academy-id 33952} {:db/id 17592186134838 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133888 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133704 :question/id #uuid "bd1f48b4-8bfc-536d-8145-0effcf44a788" :question/math-academy-id "e-9104"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "75e1da77-a5dc-5f78-977e-0d6dae99c97e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049539}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134072} {:db/id 17592186134073} {:db/id 17592186362743} {:db/id 17592186362750} {:db/id 17592186362770} {:db/id 17592186380573} {:db/id 17592186397950} {:db/id 17592186407245} {:db/id 17592186407247} {:db/id 17592186476920} {:db/id 17592186476953} {:db/id 17592186495139}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Images of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of the Matrix Under Its Action"} :step/id #uuid "f70134b1-0b93-5597-a6b6-16fdc7fb1bad" :step/math-academy-id 33937 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134840}} {:db/id 17592186134840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135112 :tutorial/content "Consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with rank $r.$ The dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of $A$ are as follows:

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) = r.$ Since the column space is the span of the columns of $A,$ its dimension is the number of linearly independent columns which, by Gaussian elimination, is $\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.
$$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^m)}_{m} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))}_{r} = m-r.
$$

Let's add these dimensions to the diagram below.

![](images/1c/1c550b87048bba6a7c362f00f09faca74ca9b056a93698436d0994c120971356.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "40af35b2-abb6-59b8-999a-9976edbb9ce8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5455 :tutorial/title "Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces"} :step/id #uuid "957cde37-32d4-515e-ad96-75c96f7bfa57" :step/math-academy-id 33951 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134837}} {:db/id 17592186135111 :tutorial/content "Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ what is the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $A?$

Note that pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$
![](images/a3/a3cf2fb6734efe387ad41c59743385154d7a172d2cc10ee0fe69ac6a7f2b342a.svg)

Therefore, by definition, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

![](images/db/dbefb436195af5ffa8841f4119054426db50ac2987138a5912991cf42321e0dc.png)

Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ by $A^T$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A^T{:}$
![](images/60/60574ae7f9fc09522e9d725c787dce63228c67e19cbef002b14e29c1f27e4b20.svg)

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^m$ under the action of $A^T$ must be $\text{Col}(A^T).$ This is also the row space of $A,$ since a linear combination of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of $A.$

![](images/c8/c82ab88289fc2d35ce354933937d908c54a9839bfa0fd126187a9723c58eeb27.png)

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b9f78c95-881f-537a-b5e6-305264553498" :question/math-academy-id "q-109777" :question/problem "Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A)$ - **II.** $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ consists of all linear combinations of the columns of $A$, that is, the rows of ${A}^{T}.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of ${A}^{T},$ it must be orthogonal to each row of ${A}^{T}.$

So, $\text{Col}(A)$ must be orthogonal to the left null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}({A}^{T}).$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of ${A}^{T},$ it must be orthogonal to each row of ${A}^{T}.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by ${A}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${A}^{T}$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}(A)$ must be orthogonal to the left null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}({A}^{T}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

I. $\text{Null}(A+B)$

II. $\text{Col}(A+B)$

III. $\text{Null}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ is the row space of $({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})^{T}=A+B.$ This consists of all linear combinations of the rows of $A+B.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of $A+B,$ it must be orthogonal to each row of $A+B.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by $A+B,$ we actually multiply each row of $A+B$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the null space of $A+B,$ which is $\text{Null}(A+B).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

Which of the following could be the equation of the polynomial above?

- $y=(x+2)(x+1)^2(x-2)$

- $y=(x+2)^3(x+1)^2(x-2)$

- $y=(x+2)(x+1)^2(x-2)^3$" :question/worked-solution "First, we notice that the function has precisely three distinct roots, $x=-2,$ $x=-1,$ and $x=2.$

Based on the graph, we can make the following conclusions about the multiplicities:

- Since the graph is *not* tangent to the $x$-axis at $x =-2,$ this root is a simple root (the multiplicity equals $1$).

- Since the graph just touches the $x$-axis and reverses direction at $x =-1,$ this root has even multiplicity.

- Since the graph passes through $x = 2,$ this root has odd multiplicity, and since the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=2,$ the multiplicity must be greater than one.

From the given options, the only possible equation is $y= (x+2)(x+1)^2(x-2)^3.$"} {:db/id 17592186517437} {:db/id 17592186129690 :question/id #uuid "554c3d5c-456e-56d6-be80-86b327875e6d" - Statement III is false. As $x$ moves left in the negative direction towards $-\infty,$ the $y$ value moves up in the positive direction towards $\infty.$

A part of the graph of a polynomial $p(x)$ is given above. Which of the following statements is true?

- $x=-4$ is a multiple root of odd multiplicity

- $x=-4$ is a multiple root of even multiplicity

- $x=-4$ is a simple root" :question/worked-solution "| Multiplicity | Sketch | Sketch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $1$

| $>1$

 Even | ![](images/9d/9d14c2588da2ee9c9f5bbc32a70791146bed609ea0d6d5912aeaa2edab02e2d7.png) | ![](images/28/28ad9248a9a509e3a44937d0438fb2366f550a22360d01b9b6a29bcac41357e8.png) |

It's possible to determine information regarding the multiplicities of the roots of a polynomial from its graph.

- If the graph intersects the $x$-axis but is *not* tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=a,$ we have a *simple* root $x=a.$

- If the graph is *tangent* to the $x$-axis at $x=a,$ we have a *multiple* root $x=a.$ Furthermore:

- If the graph touches the $x$-axis and reverses direction at $x=a,$ the multiplicity of a root $x=a$ is *even*.

- If the graph crosses the $x$-axis at $x=a,$ the multiplicity of a root $x=a$ is *odd*.

In our case, the graph is *tangent* to the $x$-axis at $x=-4.$ So, $x=-4$ is a *multiple* root. 

Furthermore, the graph touches the $x$-axis and reverses direction at $x=-4.$ So, $x=-4$ has *even* multiplicity.

Therefore, $x=-4$ is a multiple root of even multiplicity."} {:db/id 17592186048669} {:db/id 17592186518544} {:db/id 17592186129495 :question/id #uuid "7d255093-6f1a-5d48-a501-a1e3241dcefa" We summarize all possible cases in the table below:

| Multiplicity | Case 1 | Case 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ 

 (Simple root) 

 Odd | ![](images/5a/5a0221f93c65a1eeb4503604a558a6da81c4c7af81c2c52cc35ecf3d189fe99f.png) | ![](images/d5/d556b4edf39181eebb7ec87c344d6f657a6875ecd2745405eaf5351ccaff6f96.png) |
| $>1$ 

 (Multiple root) 

 Even | ![](images/9d/9d14c2588da2ee9c9f5bbc32a70791146bed609ea0d6d5912aeaa2edab02e2d7.png) | ![](images/28/28ad9248a9a509e3a44937d0438fb2366f550a22360d01b9b6a29bcac41357e8.png) |
| $>1$ 

 (Multiple root) 

 Odd | ![](images/3a/3ae81378cb3c918dd5b7730519eb5a91e949f88eef9f03f4910f4ab8fb3cd5a9.png) | ![](images/95/9506a7ce4031f1f6244c0110c3235f66ea5652bb53548a032732869cf21f5997.png) |

Note the following:

- The graph is **tangent** to the $x$-axis at multiple roots. This means that if $x=a$ is a multiple root, then the graph of the polynomial is parallel to the $x$-axis at this point.

- If the multiplicity of a root $x=a$ is *even*, the graph just touches the $x$-axis and reverses direction at $x=a.$

- If the multiplicity of a root $x=a$ is *odd* (including a simple root of multiplicity $1$), the graph crosses the $x$-axis at $x=a.$

- The graph of the polynomial is *never* tangent to the $x$-axis at simple roots." :tutorial/id #uuid "7d750148-b50a-541e-99a4-c4dcd72534bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3755 :tutorial/title 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186317035}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}, & x\in [-3,0] \\ -{x}^{2}, & x\in (0,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is converging when $x=2.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=2.$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{-}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is continuous at $x=2.$ 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
f(2)=-{2}^{2}=-4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167293 :question/id #uuid "ddf2fa7b-cdfe-5039-9760-76db03b3d4cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-342505" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "735db7a5-7bcb-5fa9-a24e-2f32aa107ab9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186511023}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186511023} :answer-field/id #uuid "790c545a-a448-5b09-a252-ea7895e22766" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186164979}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x\in [-\pi ,0] \\ 1, & x\in (0,\pi )\end{aligned}

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

$$

$$

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}\,(\frac{\pi }{2})+{f}^{+}\,(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2}=\frac{0+(-3)}{2}=-\frac{3}{2}.

:topic/math-academy-id 3198} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167938 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168045 :tutorial/content "The **Fourier convergence theorem** describes how a Fourier series behaves, especially at points where the original function is not continuous.

A Fourier series is built from smooth sine and cosine waves, so it cannot “jump” instantly the way a function with a jump discontinuity can. Instead, the series *converges* to an average value at these jumps.

More precisely, let $f(x)$ be a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function, and let its Fourier series be

$$
S(x)=\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(
a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)
\right).
$$

Then the Fourier series converges for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$. The value it converges to depends on whether $f$ is continuous at $x$.

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ the series converges to the function value:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ the series converges to the midpoint of the one-sided limits:

$$
S(x)=\dfrac{f^-(x)+f^+(x)}{2},
$$

where $f^-(x)$ and $f^+(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of $f$ at $x,$ respectively.

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "7d62d7d1-1939-536d-8fef-b02c4d023b32" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14717 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0daa028f-4325-5685-88f2-3cbbcf622af2" :step/math-academy-id 598800 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167957}} {:db/id 17592186167939 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166960 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166575 :question/id #uuid "7e478876-8258-54a8-9dd7-81978b7cf9af" :question/math-academy-id "e-21865"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5f9dcbb0-d943-5340-916e-d789b6ab03bc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048443} {:db/id 17592186049995}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167292} {:db/id 17592186167293} {:db/id 17592186317392} {:db/id 17592186317393} {:db/id 17592186317394} {:db/id 17592186317395} {:db/id 17592186317396} {:db/id 17592186317397} {:db/id 17592186375031} {:db/id 17592186375034} {:db/id 17592186375055} {:db/id 17592186432955} {:db/id 17592186432956} {:db/id 17592186432958} {:db/id 17592186480675} {:db/id 17592186480684}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Value to What a Fourier Series Converges"} :step/id #uuid "31151663-c118-573c-a32e-a71852a7ab4b" :step/math-academy-id 598801 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167940}} {:db/id 17592186167940 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168046 :tutorial/content "A powerful application of Fourier series is *evaluating infinite sums*. The strategy is to find a known Fourier series that contains the sum we want, and then choose a convenient value of $x$ to plug in.

For example, consider the function $F(x)=x^2$ defined on $x \in [-\pi,\pi).$ The Fourier series of the $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2} \cos(nx).
$$

Let's use this to find the value of the infinite sum $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2}.$ 

Now, notice that at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\cos\left(n\cdot0\right) = \cos\left(0\right) = 1.
$$

By the *pointwise convergence theorem*, since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f\left(0\right) = 0.
$$

 

Hence, we have the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}+4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\cdot 0) \\ 0 & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}+4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot 1 \\ -\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3} & =4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\ -\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{12} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2} = -\dfrac{\pi^2}{12}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8db745e6-4117-50ca-a3ea-393692db7e84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14721 :tutorial/title "Using Fourier Series For Finding Infinite Sums"} :step/id #uuid "4bdf108a-d330-5888-ae50-49c4e0f66ede" :step/math-academy-id 598804 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167941}} {:db/id 17592186167941 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166961 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166576 :question/id #uuid "0e966ca9-eab2-5443-9581-9b7cb8ecd4b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-21866"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b3cb7656-1ce6-5b6a-9e88-5ba24a943c3f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167294} {:db/id 17592186167295} {:db/id 17592186317399} {:db/id 17592186317401} {:db/id 17592186317402} {:db/id 17592186375037} {:db/id 17592186402284} {:db/id 17592186402302} {:db/id 17592186402320} {:db/id 17592186402338} {:db/id 17592186420495} {:db/id 17592186432954} {:db/id 17592186432957} {:db/id 17592186432959} {:db/id 17592186511532} {:db/id 17592186522770}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Value of an Infinite Sum Using Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "42cd3b2e-2abc-5095-b2fe-87d2a522be3b" :step/math-academy-id 598805 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167942}} {:db/id 17592186167942 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168047 :tutorial/content "Even though the Fourier series converges to the correct value at each point (using the midpoint rule at jumps), the *graphs of the partial sums* can behave strangely near a jump discontinuity.

Suppose $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x=x_0$. Then:

- The Fourier series converges at the jump to the midpoint:

$$
S(x_0)=\dfrac{f^-(x_0)+f^+(x_0)}{2}.
$$

- However, for large $N$, the partial sum

$$
S_N(x)=\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(
a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)
\right)
$$

typically *overshoots* above the higher side of the jump and *undershoots* below the lower side.

As $N$ increases, the oscillations get squeezed into a smaller neighborhood around $x_0$, but the size of the overshoot does *not* go to $0$. This persistent overshoot near jump discontinuities is called the **Gibbs phenomenon**.

For example, for the Fourier series of the $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)=x,$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi),$ the phenomenon can be observed at each point of discontinuity on the graph below.

![](images/55/55a772d1f18a80a16772e6a898917a3ad863ee33a3c5b482d9201b7d22c91089.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "c33817ab-d849-5e36-8059-f0cb3e6146cd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14722 :tutorial/title "Gibbs Phenomenon"} :step/id #uuid "bba9f02f-db71-5d7b-8afd-c5b08062d34c" :step/math-academy-id 598808} {:db/id 17592186167950 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168048 :tutorial/content "As we saw, the partial sums $S_N(x)$ appear to converge to the function $f(x)$ as $N\to\infty$. The *Fourier convergence theorem* specifies the exact value to which the series converges.

- At any point $x_0$ where $f(x)$ is *continuous*, the Fourier series converges to the function value:

$$
S(x_0)=f(x_0)
$$

- At any point $x_0$ where $f(x)$ has a *jump discontinuity*, the Fourier series converges to the midpoint of the jump (the average of the one-sided limits):

$$
S(x_0)=\dfrac{f^-(x_0)+f^+(x_0)}{2}
$$

![](images/52/5261e83960334e21396e3c7e3e2c0af82154dba29f99a338f22d5ef615d1af80.png)

For our sawtooth function above, the discontinuities occur at $x=(2k+1)\pi$. At $x=\pi$, for example, the series converges to:

$$
S(\pi)=\dfrac{f^-(\pi)+f^+(\pi)}{2} = \dfrac{\pi + (-\pi)}{2} = 0
$$

The graph of the limit function $S(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/c5/c5731fc49b0bca19ae60b9a5bc14eae5ee64f8ff36ebae85dcf2ffe0a4270708.png)

**Note:** The limit function $S(x)$ is the same as $f(x)$ except at the jump discontinuities. If $f(x)$ were continuous everywhere, then its Fourier series would converge to $f(x)$ at every point, and we could write $f(x)=S(x)$ instead of $f(x)\sim S(x)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "73760171-1fe4-5fe1-ae35-b5efeeb39cdc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14761 :tutorial/title "An Example of Convergence"} :step/id #uuid "18f33be1-5014-56eb-a799-174a9420a064" :step/math-academy-id 601089 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167939}} {:db/id 17592186167957 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168054 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $F(x)=x$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi).$ The Fourier series of its $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x) \sim S(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin\left(nx\right).
$$

The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/52/5261e83960334e21396e3c7e3e2c0af82154dba29f99a338f22d5ef615d1af80.png)

We can approximate the function $f(x)$ by summing a finite number of terms from its Fourier series. These approximations are called *partial sums*:

$$
S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\dfrac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin\left(nx\right)
$$

As $N$ increases, the partial sums match the graph of $f(x)$ more closely.

f(x) \sim \dfrac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2} \cos(nx).
$$

Let's use this to find the value of the infinite sum $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2}.$ 

Now, notice that at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\cos\left(n\cdot0\right) = \cos\left(0\right) = 1.
$$

By the *pointwise convergence theorem*, since $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f\left(0\right) = 0.
$$

 

Hence, we have the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}+4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\cdot 0) \\ 0 & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}+4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot 1 \\ -\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3} & =4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\ -\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{12} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n^2} = -\dfrac{\pi^2}{12}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8db745e6-4117-50ca-a3ea-393692db7e84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14721 :tutorial/title "Using Fourier Series For Finding Infinite Sums"} {:db/id 17592186167941 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166961 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166576 :question/id #uuid "0e966ca9-eab2-5443-9581-9b7cb8ecd4b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-21866"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b3cb7656-1ce6-5b6a-9e88-5ba24a943c3f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167294} {:db/id 17592186167295} {:db/id 17592186317399} {:db/id 17592186317401} {:db/id 17592186317402} {:db/id 17592186375037} {:db/id 17592186402284} {:db/id 17592186402302} {:db/id 17592186402320} {:db/id 17592186402338} {:db/id 17592186420495} {:db/id 17592186432954} {:db/id 17592186432957} {:db/id 17592186432959} {:db/id 17592186511532} {:db/id 17592186522770}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Value of an Infinite Sum Using Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "42cd3b2e-2abc-5095-b2fe-87d2a522be3b" :step/math-academy-id 598805 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167942}} {:db/id 17592186167942 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168047 :tutorial/content "Even though the Fourier series converges to the correct value at each point (using the midpoint rule at jumps), the *graphs of the partial sums* can behave strangely near a jump discontinuity.

Suppose $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x=x_0$. Then:

- The Fourier series converges at the jump to the midpoint:

$$
S(x_0)=\dfrac{f^-(x_0)+f^+(x_0)}{2}.
$$

- However, for large $N$, the partial sum

$$
S_N(x)=\dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(
a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)
\right)
$$

typically *overshoots* above the higher side of the jump and *undershoots* below the lower side.

As $N$ increases, the oscillations get squeezed into a smaller neighborhood around $x_0$, but the size of the overshoot does *not* go to $0$. This persistent overshoot near jump discontinuities is called the **Gibbs phenomenon**.

For example, for the Fourier series of the $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)=x,$ defined on $[-\pi,\pi),$ the phenomenon can be observed at each point of discontinuity on the graph below.

The *Fourier convergence theorem* specifies the exact value to which the series converges.

- At any point $x_0$ where $f(x)$ is *continuous*, the Fourier series converges to the function value:

$$
S(x_0)=f(x_0)
$$

- At any point $x_0$ where $f(x)$ has a *jump discontinuity*, the Fourier series converges to the midpoint of the jump (the average of the one-sided limits):

$$
S(x_0)=\dfrac{f^-(x_0)+f^+(x_0)}{2}
$$

![](images/52/5261e83960334e21396e3c7e3e2c0af82154dba29f99a338f22d5ef615d1af80.png)

For our sawtooth function above, the discontinuities occur at $x=(2k+1)\pi$. At $x=\pi$, for example, the series converges to:

$$
S(\pi)=\dfrac{f^-(\pi)+f^+(\pi)}{2} = \dfrac{\pi + (-\pi)}{2} = 0
$$

The graph of the limit function $S(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/c5/c5731fc49b0bca19ae60b9a5bc14eae5ee64f8ff36ebae85dcf2ffe0a4270708.png)

**Note:** The limit function $S(x)$ is the same as $f(x)$ except at the jump discontinuities. $$
f(x) \sim S(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin\left(nx\right).

The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/52/5261e83960334e21396e3c7e3e2c0af82154dba29f99a338f22d5ef615d1af80.png)

We can approximate the function $f(x)$ by summing a finite number of terms from its Fourier series. These approximations are called *partial sums*:

$$
S_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\dfrac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin\left(nx\right)
$$

As $N$ increases, the partial sums match the graph of $f(x)$ more closely.

![](images/4c/4c3020fcc3aa06bec65384bb3ba852b289fd1d705e554d39cc3be9b41db6623d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "dcb1351c-d635-5660-9fec-0f4c5c5f9018" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14872 :tutorial/title "An Example of Approximation"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186481706} :activity/id #uuid "3a312771-af16-5ebc-966b-7a48dcb2b02c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050989 :topic/id #uuid "7742668d-ad15-5c25-bc82-4ea5b4fd800d" :topic/math-academy-id 3198} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186481674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186480684 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "857250c9-a9b1-5080-b2c5-1728296672ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186480334}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480334} :answer-field/id #uuid "8e653195-c3d5-582e-822a-b0c443f4aade" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186480583}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ac1dfb2b-dc39-5a8f-bb78-6916e280fb3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-343361" :question/problem "$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-2, & x\in [-3,0) \\ x+1, & x\in [0,3)\end{aligned}
$$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=-3.$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $6$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=-3.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(-3) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}f(x)=4 \\ {f}^{+}(-3) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}f(x)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(-3)+{f}^{+}(-3)}{2}=\frac{4+(-2)}{2}=1.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "00120d36-1a04-5461-a0b6-aa8a3c9fb95d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481688}} {:db/id 17592186481686 :step/content {:db/id 17592186317402 :question/answer-fields $$

$$

$$

$$

F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-2x+1, & x\in [-4,0] \\ {x}^{2}+2, & x\in (0,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $8$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is converging when $x=-3.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=-3.$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $8$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is continuous at $x=-3.$ 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
f(-3)=-2(-3)+1=7.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "589a89f1-3670-5a97-9173-deba2449c324" :step/next {:db/id 17592186506635}} {:db/id 17592186506635 :step/content {:db/id 17592186317397 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a066781a-6e52-5220-93ef-23ff199bd9a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186316022}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186316022} :answer-field/id #uuid "c5f46bb7-8b99-5788-8b85-2ae0679bb181" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186317019}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cc552628-2cac-58c1-ac79-840e54e9a1ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-343390" :question/problem "$$

Now, notice that at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we have

$$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{-}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=\pi .$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(\pi ) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{-}}f(x)=1 \\ {f}^{+}(\pi ) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{+}}f(x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(\pi )+{f}^{+}(\pi )}{2}=\frac{1+0}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "5d01adcd-f270-5af1-9222-71935e9dab45" :step/next {:db/id 17592186511651}} {:db/id 17592186511651 :step/content {:db/id 17592186375034 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cb5a35bc-6e98-5466-b248-220b58805210" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186375036}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186375036} :answer-field/id #uuid "73e9342f-7d4b-572d-ae06-c85b2c42d4ba" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186375035}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8508b9f1-644b-5b60-9272-323a48701a7e" :question/math-academy-id "q-343367" :question/problem "$$

F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-4, & x\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},0) \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡x, & x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ converges when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}f(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=2 \\ {f}^{+}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{+}}f(x)=-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}\,(\frac{\pi }{2})+{f}^{+}\,(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2}=\frac{2+(-4)}{2}=-1.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "af8c258e-ccf8-5173-8bbf-21e285594589"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "735db7a5-7bcb-5fa9-a24e-2f32aa107ab9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186511023}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186511023} :answer-field/id #uuid "790c545a-a448-5b09-a252-ea7895e22766" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186164979} {:answer/id #uuid "735db7a5-7bcb-5fa9-a24e-2f32aa107ab9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186511023} {:db/id 17592186511651 :step/content {:db/id 17592186375034 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cb5a35bc-6e98-5466-b248-220b58805210" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186375036}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186375036} :answer-field/id #uuid "73e9342f-7d4b-572d-ae06-c85b2c42d4ba" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186375035}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8508b9f1-644b-5b60-9272-323a48701a7e" :question/math-academy-id "q-343367" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=\pi .$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(\pi ) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{-}}f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{+}(\pi ) & ={lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{+}}f(x)=2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to

17592186193860 :tutorial/content "We can always represent the solution of an inequality using a number line.

For example, let's express the solution of the following inequality using a number line:

$$
5x \geq 30
$$

The variable $x$ is being *multiplied* by $5.$ To isolate $x,$ we can perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $5.$ So, we divide both sides of the inequality by $5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & \ge 30 \\ \frac{5x}{5} & \ge \frac{30}{5} \\ \frac{5x}{5} & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $5$ from the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5x}{5} & \ge 6 \\ \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} & \ge 6 \\ x & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \geq 6.$ This solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

Therefore, we can find the axis of symmetry of a parabola by finding the roots and then taking their average value. 

So, if the roots are $x_1$ and $x_2,$ the **average of the roots formula** tells us that the axis of symmetry of the parabola is

$$
x = \dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}.
$$

For example, let's consider the parabola 

$$
y=(x+2)(x-4).
$$

We have the roots $x_1=-2$ and $x_2=4.$ Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{-2+4}{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=(x+2)(x-4)$ is $x=1,$ as shown below.

If we know two points on a parabola with *identical* $y$-values, we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking an average of the two $x$-values. 

For example, consider the parabola $y=f(x)$ above. Notice that the values of $f(x)$ at the points $x=-3$ and $x=5$ are equal.

$$
f(-3) = f(5) = 3
$$

Therefore, the parabola's axis of symmetry must be equidistant from the lines $x=-3$ and $x=5.$ We can find this by taking the average of these two values.

If the parabola's vertex is $(h,k),$ then we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =\frac{-3+5}{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $h=1$ is the $x$-coordinate of the vertex, and the axis of symmetry of the parabola is $x=1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "23d4f6e0-c0a7-5551-bd88-80b3268a5b2b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13792 :tutorial/title "Extending the Formula"} :step/id #uuid "1b132072-c297-50ce-be49-d3a763e0a32f" :step/math-academy-id 502439 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111697}} {:db/id 17592186111697 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110728 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110373 :question/id #uuid "04877936-271e-5fcb-a1ea-aa39c52482b6" :question/math-academy-id "e-19740"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9a2eed2b-7f94-5b53-bc5c-4bf9aea18d32" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048398}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111153} {:db/id 17592186111154} {:db/id 17592186541070} {:db/id 17592186541071} {:db/id 17592186563654} {:db/id 17592186563659} {:db/id 17592186563728} {:db/id 17592186563739} {:db/id 17592186563740}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Vertex of a Parabola From Table Data"} :step/id #uuid "f7518575-386c-57e6-893c-6238e3cc01a1" :step/math-academy-id 502440}] :activity/title "The Average of the Roots Formula" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186110824} {:db/id 17592186111692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111921 :tutorial/content "If a parabola has two roots, the axis of symmetry occurs precisely halfway between the roots of the parabola. If we know two points on a parabola with *identical* $y$-values, we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking an average of the two $x$-values. 

For example, consider the parabola $y=f(x)$ above. Notice that the values of $f(x)$ at the points $x=-3$ and $x=5$ are equal.

$$
f(-3) = f(5) = 3
$$

Therefore, the parabola's axis of symmetry must be equidistant from the lines $x=-3$ and $x=5.$ We can find this by taking the average of these two values.

If the parabola's vertex is $(h,k),$ then we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =\frac{-3+5}{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, given the matrix 
![](images/ad/addf5cd1e1219a1e1ce28f3d27d1b000b3a99640ff89a62e55b66f3a5cdb3521.svg)
which is in row echelon form, let's find the pivots of $A.$

- The first non-zero entry in the first row is the entry $a_{11}=1.$ So this is a pivot.

- The first non-zero entry of the second row is $a_{22}=1.$ So this is also a pivot.

- The first non-zero entry in the third row is $a_{34}=1.$ Therefore this is a pivot.

![](images/96/96dcf8cf9f0d387e0539ea04dd7ae4a498534361ad6bd5ed3bb119ae21f0416a.svg)

The **pivot columns** of a matrix in row echelon form are simply the columns in which the pivots appear.

For our matrix $A$, we can see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns.

The non-pivot columns are the columns that do not contain a pivot. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}_{xy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

To find ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y)+{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =4x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Finally, we find ${f}_{xyx}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xy}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{xy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124948 :question/id #uuid "83167862-effb-539c-8ffb-5705b88d44f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-36019"} {:db/id 17592186268922 :question/id #uuid "e5449d51-c794-5d29-87ea-e1688a095f9f" :question/math-academy-id "q-132940"} {:db/id 17592186268923 :question/id #uuid "01b2f238-4be0-502a-a439-500d85cd72b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-132961" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00508df2-67fc-5789-9478-c3e2d42771e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186266152} {:answer/id #uuid "44da4fc7-1df8-536a-a190-f8c23a3e32f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\pi " :db/id 17592186266758} {:answer/id #uuid "63a9b984-28e7-58d3-8128-0a6d4ca98f26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186267021} {:answer/id #uuid "88f1885b-f866-5cf3-96ea-874e43e6a210" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186267363} {:answer/id #uuid "8ebfbd8f-e225-52f2-af81-73501dcd099d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186267416}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186266152} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f17d030-5507-55e9-8f15-4689404588ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268545}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Evaluate ${f}_{xxz}(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi )$ for $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡xyz) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\cdot yz \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{xx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{x}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =yz\cdot (-yz\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xx}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({f}_{xx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}\cdot (2z\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)+xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)) \\  & =-{y}^{2}z(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)+xyz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz))\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)$ at $(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(1,\frac{1}{2},\pi ) & =-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\cdot \pi \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi )+1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi )) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{4}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268924 :question/id #uuid "5eef046b-e675-5de1-b784-361653847836" :question/math-academy-id "q-132984"} {:db/id 17592186335787 :question/id #uuid "101d6e00-46ae-511e-8fb6-40ece63bbd97" :question/math-academy-id "q-65068"} {:db/id 17592186335788 :question/id #uuid "ab0f3803-2840-52ec-8174-767389c2fcc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-65071" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0548138d-e543-5a54-a872-c6505ae35f31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186333031} {:answer/id #uuid "3dd21545-2656-5f34-8899-9e63ce0f1a99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2y}{x}" :db/id 17592186333573} {:answer/id #uuid "56f12986-c08d-5855-9c32-e38ca3128af3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186333777} {:answer/id #uuid "7279d9a1-e1cd-5962-b045-74040fa8edd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y}{4x}" :db/id 17592186334026} {:answer/id #uuid "810185ca-f52f-5e5b-a85b-df54ad11e6a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{4+y}{x}" :db/id 17592186334135}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186333031} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7a6c17f-ff74-5dd2-941a-c73839c7e4a2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186335605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Calculate ${f}_{yxx}(x,y)$ given that $f(x,y)={y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =2y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})) \\  & =2y\cdot \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${f}_{yxx}(x,y)$ by differentiating ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =xy\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)) \\  & =\frac{xy}{x+y+z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zy}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{z}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{xy}{x+y+z}) \\  & =\frac{x\cdot (x+y+z)-xy\cdot (1)}{(x+y+z)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+xy+xz-xy}{(x+y+z)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+xz}{(x+y+z)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{zy}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}+xz}{(x+y+z)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)\cdot (x+y+z)^{2}-({x}^{2}+xz)\cdot (2(x+y+z)\cdot 1)}{(x+y+z)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{(2x+z)(x+y+z)-2({x}^{2}+xz)}{(x+y+z)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{zyx}(x,y,z)$ at $(1,1,-1):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyx}(1,1,-1) & =\frac{(2(1)+(-1))(1+1+(-1))-2({1}^{2}+1(-1))}{(1+1+(-1))^{3}}=\frac{(1)(1)-2(0)}{(1)^{3}}=1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049696} {:db/id 17592186051072} {:db/id 17592186051048 :topic/difficulty 0.714468048926131 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428474 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. "Determine the stationary point of $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+4xy+{y}^{2}+4y.$" :question/worked-solution "The stationary points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T},$ where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}.
$$

In tihs case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =4x+4y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =4x+2y+4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+4y & 4x+2y+4\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the stationary points, we need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$
Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+4y &=0 \\ 4x+2y+4 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving for $x$ in the first equation, we get

$$
4x+4y=0\,⟹\,x=-y.
$$

Then, substituting $x=-y$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-y)+2y+4 & =0 \\ -4y+2y+4 & =0 \\ -2y & =-4 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting this value into $x=-y,$ we obtain

$$
y=2\,⟹\,x=-2.
$$

Therefore, our system has one solution, $(-2,2).$

In conclusion, $f$ has one stationary point, $(-2,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186511526 :question/id #uuid "8d70bf0e-d43a-5715-a8f9-251ae990c8fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-103926"} {:db/id 17592186511549 :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452757}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$ 
has the second derivative

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}y{e}^{x} & {e}^{x}-{e}^{y} \\ {e}^{x}-{e}^{y} & -x{e}^{y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

and has a stationary point at $(1,1).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $H(1,1)>0$
- **II.** $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,1)>0$
- **III.** The point $(1,1)$ is a local maximum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}e & 0 \\ 0 & -e\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(1,1),$ we get

$$
H(1,1)=det({f}^{″}(1,1))=e\cdot (-e)-{0}^{2}=-{e}^{2}<0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,1)=({f}^{″}(1,1))_{11}=e>0.$

- Statement III is false. Since $H(1,1)<0,$ the point $(1,1)$ is a saddle point by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186364681 :question/id #uuid "a2adfa73-7e18-5d5d-8163-694e5efa8a14" :question/math-academy-id "q-104980"} {:db/id 17592186368784 :question/id #uuid "7ba712ba-8939-58aa-ab47-15caf19c7eaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-81165"} {:db/id 17592186368791 :question/id #uuid "8ce3eb01-5fdc-5cad-ba01-77459c09b714" :question/math-academy-id "q-81166"} {:db/id 17592186420504 :question/id #uuid "d1a7556c-36af-5f0b-b64c-a00089e6850e" :question/math-academy-id "q-37456"} {:db/id 17592186434983 :question/id #uuid "b007310c-a11f-531c-b695-1febe8ef0462" :question/math-academy-id "q-37589"} {:db/id 17592186520472 :question/id #uuid "60652dd5-fdd9-5974-9d65-a71597afa3f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-104994" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b6b1671-0717-5482-8d52-d0c250e890fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186520056} {:answer/id #uuid "3bef4c65-0c4b-5059-b575-1485beb2844b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186520076} {:answer/id #uuid "63cd11be-33ac-578f-99a4-b5fbfef6ba96" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186520145} {:answer/id #uuid "862feb99-123c-5810-b1cc-80efe435e8f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186520187} {:answer/id #uuid "d30d25a2-0e79-557a-a62e-539de549b8be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186520288}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520076} :answer-field/id #uuid "06c9a2bb-e41c-52c6-8b2c-a83b5dffeaf4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186520368}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the first derivative

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],
$$

and has a stationary point at $(3,-3).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(3,-3)>0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)<0$

III. The point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x+2y-6,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y-6)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+2y)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,-3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,-3)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(3,-3),$ we get

$$
H(3,-3)=det({f}^{″}(3,-3))=4\cdot 2-{2}^{2}=4>0.
$$

- Statement II is false. We have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)=({f}^{″}(3,-3))_{11}=4>0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(3,-3)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)>0,$ the point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186520514 :question/id #uuid "f7f93cc0-fc36-5de6-903e-61c89b0db59c" :question/math-academy-id "q-105213" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29711ca7-b3cc-53ec-bec7-d90a0aeb16e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186520050} {:answer/id #uuid "3df5a0e2-1ea8-5fe2-a697-20a5c5faa39f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186520080} {:answer/id #uuid "cc0ee0e0-9a43-5369-b3d7-8e3c43d21d2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186520275} {:answer/id #uuid "ce672a55-9e57-56eb-a86f-0f1f3507439c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186520280} {:answer/id #uuid "ec9f7794-bd99-5638-b872-bfdbc7829cf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186520339}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520280} :answer-field/id #uuid "6b0046f1-2976-582a-85ca-24a28e09b21d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186520398}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the first derivative

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],
$$

and has a stationary point at $(-1,1).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(-1,1)<0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0$

III. The point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})=\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & -\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1,1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(-1,1),$ we get

$$
H(-1,1)=det({f}^{″}(-1,1))=(-2)^{2}-(-1)^{2}=3>0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)=({f}^{″}(-1,1))_{11}=-2<0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(-1,1)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0,$ the point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186534985 :question/id #uuid "22b41189-2cbf-5d3c-9c30-272b9cf4d5e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-104972" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13af5318-875b-5713-b76b-c620f034eee7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186534308} {:answer/id #uuid "6c1d85e8-0bc7-546d-befe-bf2f6875ee46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186534489} {:answer/id #uuid "6da12e8f-9a72-519d-aa8c-c280dab33816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186534492} {:answer/id #uuid "73c89adb-6ad9-5a52-805c-8e998406f119" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186534515} {:answer/id #uuid "9e958518-516a-5fe5-b01c-caeda1f4b877" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186534621}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186534621} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ca90436-78d3-5958-bb30-5ff0939b26c6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186534918}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The function

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=x\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=y\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2})=(1+{x}^{2}){e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2})=(1+{y}^{2}){e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2})=xy\text{ }\,{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})/2}\end{aligned}

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1,$ and determine which of the following statements is true." :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1 &=0 \\ x+3y+5 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get

$$
H(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$"} {:db/id 17592186125084 :question/id #uuid "e71f4d1b-7ab2-518d-aa98-4d69ed0f6542" :question/math-academy-id "q-37592" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "114d029d-432f-5d2d-a8e0-da4352b9cbe0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local maximum at $(2,2)$" :db/id 17592186520012} {:answer/id #uuid "5e1b31e7-050e-5530-973b-420e7f556047" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(2,2)$" :db/id 17592186520137} {:answer/id #uuid "8a1bf858-df10-5d12-842f-190930cca500" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$" :db/id 17592186520195} {:answer/id #uuid "a61d9d31-5126-5495-bb34-7b540584d0e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0)$ and a saddle point at $(-2,-2)$" :db/id 17592186520217} {:answer/id #uuid "da384a82-fb82-524f-a94b-1ea107ebde1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(0,0)$ and a local maximum at $(-2,-2)$" :db/id 17592186520300}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520137} :answer-field/id #uuid "d3b332ce-1536-5642-87d8-20b5ef880b58" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123104}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-6y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-6x.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y &=0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-6x &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
3{x}^{2}-6y=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})}^{2}-6x & =0 \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{4}-8x & =0 \\ x({x}^{3}-8) & =0 \\ x & =0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
x=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}=0,\,\,x=2\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}=2.
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=6x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=-6 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=-6\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=6y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6x & -6 \\ -6 & 6y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=0\cdot 0-(-6)^{2}=-36<0.
$$

Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2,2)=[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(2,2),$ we get

$$
H(2,2)=det({f}^{″}(2,2))=12\cdot 12-(-6)^{2}=108>0.
$$

Finally, since $H(2,2)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,2)=({f}^{″}(2,2))_{11}=12>0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(2,2).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(2,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186241041 :question/id #uuid "9136d3e6-f2a0-5b9c-a6a2-efe0a42ad6ee" :question/math-academy-id "q-105335" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2083fb67-822f-5c61-a364-c7c9d194031b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(4,0)$ and a local maximum at $(3,1)$" :db/id 17592186238338} {:answer/id #uuid "2d567df9-25a8-5d23-8121-d47039a7f3a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(1,0)$ and a local maximum at $(5,-4)$" :db/id 17592186238456} {:answer/id #uuid "6248101c-5576-5662-a6e6-9e82ed11cdba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,0)$ and a local maximum at $(5,-4)$" :db/id 17592186238920} {:answer/id #uuid "9657dc67-31a7-5307-b0a3-970644a18023" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,0)$ and a saddle point at $(5,-4)$" :db/id 17592186239356} {:answer/id #uuid "a885e205-57e3-5ddd-bba6-1c3c5468b96a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(4,0)$ and a local minimum at $(3,1)$" :db/id 17592186239522}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186238456} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d816319-57a5-5bfb-bdbc-1674489ced59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186240415}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}4-4y-4x & 4-4x+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}4-4y-4x & 4-4x+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4-4y-4x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=4-4x+{y}^{2}.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4-4y-4x &=0 \\ 4-4x+{y}^{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $x,$ we get

$$
4-4y-4x=0\,⟹\,x=1-y.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4-4(1-y)+{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}+4y & =0 \\ y(y+4) & =0 \\ y & =-4,0.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $x=1-y,$ we obtain

$$
y=-4\,⟹\,x=1-(-4)=5,\,\,y=0\,\,\,\,\,\,⟹\,x=1-0=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,0)$ and $(5,-4)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-4y-4x)=-4\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-4x+{y}^{2})=-4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-4y-4x)=-4\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-4x+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$

$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-y & 8{y}^{2}-x\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-y & 8{y}^{2}-x\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={x}^{2}-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=8{y}^{2}-x.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-y &=0 \\ 8{y}^{2}-x &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{2}-y=0\,⟹\,y={x}^{2}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{({x}^{2})}^{2}-x & =0 \\ 8{x}^{4}-x & =0 \\ x(8{x}^{3}-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y={x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
x=0\,\,\,\,⟹\,y={0}^{2}=0,\,\,x=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,y={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y)=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{y}^{2}-x)=-1 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y)=-1\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{y}^{2}-x)=16y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2x & -1 \\ -1 & 16y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))={0}^{2}-(-1)^{2}=-1<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}),$ we get

$$
H(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})=det({f}^{″}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}))=1\cdot 4-(-1)^{2}=3>0
$$

Finally, since $H(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})={h}_{11}=1>0.$ Therefore, we have a local minimum at $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}).$"} {:db/id 17592186399475 :question/id #uuid "e1b5f6e8-a9c9-5be3-86f7-77f082bfcf04" :question/math-academy-id "q-105338"} {:db/id 17592186434981 :question/id #uuid "05076731-f2b5-5426-b032-1f0962af8ee1" :question/math-academy-id "q-105278"} {:db/id 17592186434982 :question/id #uuid "0a336a18-c506-59a2-baef-25499733a8d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-81179" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c27e9b4e-206f-5150-a881-d37dde9c4e85" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(3,1)$ and a local maximum $(-3,-1)$" :db/id 17592186434966} {:answer/id #uuid "d2284ea7-6bfd-52fc-b08e-cbc5dc03d189" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-3,1)$ and a local minimum $(-3,1)$" :db/id 17592186434969} {:answer/id #uuid "e02c6dc0-e019-5937-b18e-930a68cb954f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(3,1)$ and a local maximum $(-3,-1)$" :db/id 17592186434971} {:answer/id #uuid "e957c6c0-0532-521e-b2c3-2747f7ac1033" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(-3,1)$ and a saddle point at $(-3,1)$" :db/id 17592186434972} {:answer/id #uuid "f5d5c20b-2412-5e45-a4e7-034876616c97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has saddle points at $(3,1)$ and $(-3,-1)$" :db/id 17592186434975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186434975} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce8b2aa5-8481-5045-bb5b-59aa8a2d0aa3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186434979}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:
