"Given that 
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{bmatrix},$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(\pi ,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\end{bmatrix},$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))=-{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy) \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))=-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy) & -{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(\pi ,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(\pi ,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(\pi ,-1)=0\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot (-1)=-1.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "098d6e52-39b3-522b-84c5-e656d2477a6a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481463}} {:db/id 17592186481451 :step/content {:db/id 17592186351196 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a863fee-48cb-518a-94c7-332f0d5dfb90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186348671} {:answer/id #uuid "236352e1-e284-5137-93e8-01d0c0b82dd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186348749} {:answer/id #uuid "cd6da9cd-0b80-5391-a066-ff87ff441cbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186350254} {:answer/id #uuid "d5b5d5ad-403a-5e9b-b47e-9495ed54eecd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186350322} {:answer/id #uuid "da828216-6cb2-53d2-9a0c-74a4b4c5a870" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186350365}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350365} :answer-field/id #uuid "0f56bbbf-1a13-5c6d-a2d7-69c5469daa32" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350734}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0dab700a-fa4f-5675-9473-37a2b428ee20" :question/math-academy-id "q-81023" :question/problem "Given that

evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2(x-1){y}^{2} & 2(x-1)^{2}y\end{bmatrix},$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2(x-1){y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2(x-1)^{2}y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x-1){y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x-1)^{2}y)=4(x-1)y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x-1){y}^{2})=4(x-1)y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x-1)^{2}y)=2(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2} & 4(x-1)y \\ 4(x-1)y & 2(x-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,1)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(0,1)=2\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-12.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4e33b2ed-2bc9-51ba-9064-eab461a12ff8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481454}} {:db/id 17592186481454 :step/content {:db/id 17592186481414 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "93574e00-8aff-52c2-8fef-8d24d76bb02a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186481016} {:answer/id #uuid "aee9d420-4960-50a5-922a-c43137c76d7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186481067} {:answer/id #uuid "bc4a4294-c877-56f6-bfd0-3109ee79c13c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186481097} {:answer/id #uuid "c00142a0-9805-5734-8860-3bf5256f853f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186481104} {:answer/id #uuid "e631a5f0-8bc9-5fbb-b72c-fddfe67625ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186481177}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481177} :answer-field/id #uuid "3cad98c5-f0af-530e-9545-f63d666cd3ea" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481264}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c02d4f47-274a-5db8-9775-386bac66028f" :question/math-academy-id "q-102684" :question/problem "Find ${f}^{″}(1,2)$ for the function $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{y}{x} & \operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x})=-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x})=\frac{1}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,2).$ This gives

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "63ea7e02-9f7a-5a09-b718-d06795e4cb97" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481442}} {:db/id 17592186481455 :step/content {:db/id 17592186157541 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2fca28ad-f59e-5a0a-bb4c-0662386d1e94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186480829} {:answer/id #uuid "3075a971-db98-5b66-a3d1-9af12fdf7be7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186480831} {:answer/id #uuid "8cb3995c-cc62-5136-82b2-472b0cb824be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186481006} {:answer/id #uuid "d0ef3863-4e52-56dd-9984-66598e15e8ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186481130} {:answer/id #uuid "dc10b03f-56c5-527c-94f1-47709864755a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186481155}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481006} :answer-field/id #uuid "28c26c69-61cb-5d08-9210-43f100a3d7fe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186153490}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "cd7463fc-6818-5da6-ab8a-b593c73ec670" :question/math-academy-id "q-102699" :question/problem "Find ${f}^{″}(1,0)$ for the function $f(x,y)=xy-{x}^{2}{y}^{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.

${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x} & 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix},$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x})=-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=\frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x})=\frac{2y}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}

evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{y}^{2}}{x} & 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix},$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x})=-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=\frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{x})=\frac{2y}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ \frac{2y}{x} & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=(-1)\cdot 0-2\cdot 2=-4.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a882a718-46ae-5afd-bb1b-85e1be5639e2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481455}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a863fee-48cb-518a-94c7-332f0d5dfb90" :answer/type {:db/id $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{y}{x} & \operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x})=-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x})=\frac{1}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,2).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,2)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "63ea7e02-9f7a-5a09-b718-d06795e4cb97" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481442}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "93574e00-8aff-52c2-8fef-8d24d76bb02a" :answer/type {:db/id $f(x,y)=xy-{x}^{2}{y}^{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-{x}^{2}{y}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-{x}^{2}{y}^{3})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}y-2x{y}^{3} & x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-2x{y}^{3})=-2{y}^{3}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})=1-6x{y}^{2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-2x{y}^{3})=1-6x{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})=-6{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}-2{y}^{3} & 1-6x{y}^{2} \\ 1-6x{y}^{2} & -6{x}^{2}y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(1,0).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,0)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5b55b18c-139d-56b5-94eb-26aeb293ef39" :question/math-academy-id "q-80947" :question/problem "Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={e}^{xy}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy})={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})={e}^{xy}+xy\,\text{ }{e}^{xy}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{xy})={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} & {e}^{xy}(1+xy) \\ {e}^{xy}(1+xy) & {x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3f710bff-ad8f-52f4-b629-314c5a07298d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186527281}} {:db/id 17592186527252 :step/content {:db/id 17592186527148 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "376b6d35-c19b-56a0-93ca-9e64900695ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-24" :db/id 17592186526607} {:answer/id #uuid "4d63a9d4-f48b-551f-a330-cb4773261398" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186526660} {:answer/id #uuid "57cd56c0-cc2d-5c47-9c19-0fd322aee1ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186526683} {:answer/id #uuid "7f6fbe7f-9b92-59d9-8aed-d5539feec274" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16" :db/id 17592186526755} {:answer/id #uuid "d5b9d20a-a2bf-5378-921c-e265c88f998e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186526914}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186526755} :answer-field/id #uuid "905b588f-0f57-5923-a81f-afb037b87739" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186527074}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "33021c77-54f7-572b-82bd-06940f46518d" :question/math-academy-id "q-102691" :question/problem "Given that 
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det({f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}2x{y}^{2}-2x & 2y{x}^{2}\end{aligned}],$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}-2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=2{y}^{2}-2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{x}^{2})=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-2x)=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{x}^{2})=2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-1)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,-1)=0\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)=-16.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "53935bee-25ea-5d48-bdee-5940866bf3d1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186527286}} {:db/id 17592186527271 :step/content {:db/id 17592186430445 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "007fcd15-219d-5a7b-979f-5872cbdb9291" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{x}{y} \\ \frac{x}{y} & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430414} {:answer/id #uuid "157d76c9-2e6f-5cdb-897c-847f29e94391" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{x}{y} \\ \frac{x}{y} & -\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430417} {:answer/id #uuid "349923f1-1f51-5fc6-9589-ada6acd4c3c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430423} {:answer/id #uuid "7529d158-9818-51d1-bf9e-38fc8f2bbd6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{x}{y} \\ \frac{x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430429} {:answer/id #uuid "ea727c2d-0baf-5e14-8734-e9b51371b264" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & -\frac{x}{y}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430438}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186430423} :answer-field/id #uuid "eca99a2b-d50a-519b-aef0-e2b86f3c4cf7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186430443}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "98de8580-5081-5c82-af81-6826d2545a45" :question/math-academy-id "q-102461" :question/problem "Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9e95f518-b55f-5878-93c7-26bfeaacd14e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186527252}} {:db/id 17592186527281 :step/content {:db/id 17592186351229 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0379a8f3-5c08-5a0e-9aa9-ee7247f5bb7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186348479} {:answer/id #uuid "0f2c18f5-f6c6-5cb7-9bd3-ef891a719882" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2y & 0 \\ 0 & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186348580} {:answer/id #uuid "235323a0-a480-5c75-9639-2308eb39664a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2xy \\ 2xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186348748} {:answer/id #uuid "3438c329-ab2c-5701-840d-707e4cfa738f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2y \\ 2y & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186348915} {:answer/id #uuid "703d071f-0017-59ad-ade4-9601ec2c639e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2} & 4xy \\ 4xy & 2({x}^{2}-1)\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186349481}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186349481} :answer-field/id #uuid "1892be87-58b9-5f45-a8a1-451663b051c5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350749}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "235e87ab-40f0-5bca-9e1d-4479ce5e2de8" :question/math-academy-id "q-81119" :question/problem "Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1)) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}({x}^{2}-1))\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{2} & 2y({x}^{2}-1)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2})=2{y}^{2}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=4xy \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2})=4xy\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y({x}^{2}-1))=2({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det(\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x))

In our case, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=4x-6y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4x-6y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=-6x\end{aligned}

$$

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "64116d30-10df-5392-b872-327ec4131913" :question/math-academy-id "q-163642" :question/problem "Given that 
${f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}4xy-3{y}^{2} & 2{x}^{2}-6xy\end{bmatrix},$ 
evaluate the Hessian determinant of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The Hessian determinant $H(x,y)$ is the determinant of the second derivative:

$$
H(x)=det(\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x))
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, notice that since
$\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}4xy-3{y}^{2} & 2{x}^{2}-6xy\end{bmatrix},$
we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4xy-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}-6xy.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=4x-6y \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-3{y}^{2})=4x-6y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-6xy)=-6x\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4y & 4x-6y \\ 4x-6y & -6x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{″}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -2 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
H(1,1)=4\cdot (-6)-(-2)\cdot (-2)=-28.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f0dacf22-0476-588e-ab05-d59e8b40b421"} {:db/id 17592186527271 :step/content {:db/id 17592186430445 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "007fcd15-219d-5a7b-979f-5872cbdb9291" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{x}{y} \\ \frac{x}{y} & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430414} {:answer/id #uuid "157d76c9-2e6f-5cdb-897c-847f29e94391" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{x}{y} \\ \frac{x}{y} & -\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430417} {:answer/id #uuid "349923f1-1f51-5fc6-9589-ada6acd4c3c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430423} {:answer/id #uuid "7529d158-9818-51d1-bf9e-38fc8f2bbd6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{x}{y} \\ \frac{x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430429} {:answer/id #uuid "ea727c2d-0baf-5e14-8734-e9b51371b264" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & -\frac{x}{y}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186430438}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186430423} :answer-field/id #uuid "eca99a2b-d50a-519b-aef0-e2b86f3c4cf7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186430443}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "98de8580-5081-5c82-af81-6826d2545a45" :question/math-academy-id "q-102461" :question/problem "Find ${f}^{″}(x,y)$ for the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y.$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & \frac{x}{y}-1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{1}{y}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}-1)=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{1}{y} & -\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9e95f518-b55f-5878-93c7-26bfeaacd14e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186527252}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "007fcd15-219d-5a7b-979f-5872cbdb9291" :answer/type {:db/id :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049676 :topic/id #uuid "0a177390-6525-5d0c-8721-f7f75db39408" :topic/math-academy-id 1945} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

One way is to consider the Taylor expansion of $f$ about $\mathbf{a}{:}$

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots
$$

Since $\mathbf{a}$ is a stationary point, we have $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T.$ This gives

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots.
$$

Let's assume that $\mathbf x$ is close to $\mathbf a,$ $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0,$ and that the terms of cubic order and higher are sufficiently small. Then, we have

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}).
$$

Recall that $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is an $n \times n$ *symmetric* matrix. Thus, the term

$$
(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

is a *quadratic form*.

Therefore, we note the following:

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, this quadratic form is always positive, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) > 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) > f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *minimum*.

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, this quadratic form is always negative, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) < 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) < f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *maximum.*

- If this quadratic form is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point.

The assumption $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0$ is important. If $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) =0,$ then the quadratic form is zero along some line through $\mathbf a$ or zero *everywhere* in a neighborhood of $\mathbf a.$ In such cases, we cannot ignore the higher-order terms and must use another method to classify the critical point.

Analogously with functions of one variable, we have the following definitions:

44846 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125486}} {:db/id 17592186125628 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125873 :tutorial/content "Now, recall the definition of local extrema for single-variable functions:

- A function $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x$-values in a neighborhood of $a.$

- A function $f(x)$ has a local maximum at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x$-values in a neighborhood of $a.$

On the function's graph, a local minimum is the lowest point of a valley, and a local maximum is the highest point of a peak.

![](images/ba/ba5be082363bd963514baa6b1a777f02098d53a3b0a80ddc2fad231e4669ebd7.png)

We can generalize the concept of local extrema to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ as follows:

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a local minimum at the point $\mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x}$ in a neighborhood of $\mathbf{a}.$

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a local maximum at the point $\mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x}$ in a neighborhood of $\mathbf{a}.$

In particular, for a function $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R},$ local minima and maxima are the lowest points in valleys and highest points in peaks, respectively, in the graph $z=f(x,y)$ of the function.

![](images/74/74d04165fd3bd5cd24ae82351bbf840e7d549b272c3deea16671dbfcd40bc75a.png)

For the points $A$ and $B,$ we can take neighborhoods of the $(x,y)$-values at these points such that $A$ and $B$ are the lowest points on the graph in these neighborhoods. Hence, they are local minima.

Similarly, for the points $C$ and $D,$ we can take neighborhoods of the $(x,y)$-values at these points such that $C$ and $D$ are the highest points on the graph in these neighborhoods. Hence, they are local maxima.

**Note**: For the point $E,$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f(x_E,y_E) = f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ or $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$, the point $E$ satisfies the conditions for a local minimum *and* a local maximum.

Finally, the points $F$ and $G$ are neither local minima nor local maxima. Notice that any neighborhood of $F$ will contain both points that lie higher than $F$ and lower than $F$ on the graph (similarly, for the point $G$)." :tutorial/id #uuid "fc6789c5-925e-54f4-9a5a-bfb179e77937" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7752 :tutorial/title "Local Extrema of a Multivariable Function"} :step/id #uuid "086acac3-3967-5f92-bf6e-ae6524a36328" :step/math-academy-id 44870 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125626}} {:db/id 17592186125629 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124648 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124211 :question/id #uuid "94c54743-ba74-51c5-9c59-777125bb76f6" :question/math-academy-id "e-12465"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "233eab4c-ab17-53a8-ae03-f6f28ac78922" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048555} {:db/id 17592186048786} {:db/id 17592186048883}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124820} {:db/id 17592186124823} {:db/id 17592186284417} {:db/id 17592186284420} {:db/id 17592186284421} {:db/id 17592186284422} {:db/id 17592186367874} {:db/id 17592186401419} {:db/id 17592186434751} {:db/id 17592186434752} {:db/id 17592186434753} {:db/id 17592186434760}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Local Extrema Using Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ab662d13-5448-5cfa-8e5b-f6bf4d245b75" :step/math-academy-id 44871 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125487}} {:db/id 17592186125630 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125874 :tutorial/content "Recall the following definitions for single-variable functions:

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global minimum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global maximum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

On the function's graph, the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points, respectively.

![](images/63/633526565293f480a6a5fc45b87a70d38e946ae0f72a925f0074776e201a43a4.png)

We can generalize this concept to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global minimum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global minimum** of the function, the smallest value the function attains on its domain.

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global maximum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global maximum** of the function, the largest value the function attains on its domain.

In particular, for a function $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R},$ the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points on the graph $z=f(x,y),$ respectively.

![](images/de/de4cfc96fdce210430291999e5997f4a0c39ed1fbe63c3848b61508ca3f04114.png)

For the function shown above:

- The minimum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = -2,$ so the global minimum is $-2,$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,-1).$ Therefore the global minimum point is $(1,-1,-2).$

- Similarly, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = 2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,1).$ Therefore the global maximum point is $(1,1,2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c71de7-b70c-5b7f-a566-143fd897ff59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d367e806-9c4c-5d98-bc43-97c56882eee8" :step/math-academy-id 44876 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125625}} {:db/id 17592186125645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125885 :tutorial/content "To summarize, the point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a stationary point of the function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ if $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T,$ and we can classify $\mathbf{a}$ as follows:

- The minimum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = -2,$ so the global minimum is $-2,$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,-1).$ Therefore the global minimum point is $(1,-1,-2).$

- Similarly, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = 2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,1).$ Therefore the global maximum point is $(1,1,2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c71de7-b70c-5b7f-a566-143fd897ff59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d367e806-9c4c-5d98-bc43-97c56882eee8" :step/math-academy-id 44876 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125625}} {:db/id 17592186125485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

One way is to consider the Taylor expansion of $f$ about $\mathbf{a}{:}$

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots
$$

Since $\mathbf{a}$ is a stationary point, we have $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T.$ This gives

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots.
$$

Let's assume that $\mathbf x$ is close to $\mathbf a,$ $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0,$ and that the terms of cubic order and higher are sufficiently small. Then, we have

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}).
$$

Recall that $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is an $n \times n$ *symmetric* matrix. Thus, the term

$$
(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

is a *quadratic form*.

Therefore, we note the following:

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, this quadratic form is always positive, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) > 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) > f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *minimum*.

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, this quadratic form is always negative, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) < 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) < f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *maximum.*

- If this quadratic form is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point.

The assumption $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0$ is important. If $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) =0,$ then the quadratic form is zero along some line through $\mathbf a$ or zero *everywhere* in a neighborhood of $\mathbf a.$ In such cases, we cannot ignore the higher-order terms and must use another method to classify the critical point.

In the work that follows, we will only consider cases where $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3cedcd0c-77c7-5789-b76d-7ae3307c237b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4263 :tutorial/title "Classifying Local Extrema Using Taylor Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "f3f90cb9-acd8-5630-859d-3bd37e502189" :step/math-academy-id 25915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125645}} {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

![](images/b5/b5dfe5fbad89ef3c6231dafe40d719be1faf007f782342abd6475756eda97b1e.svg)

Analogously with functions of one variable, we have the following definitions:

- A point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is a **critical point** of $f$ if $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ or does not exist.

- Critical points where $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ are known as **stationary points.**

The local extrema of a function $f$ occur at the critical points. So, we can find the local extrema of $f$ by determining the stationary points *and* the points where $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ does not exist and classify them accordingly (we'll discuss how to do this shortly). 

Not all of the solutions of $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ give rise to local extrema! Solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ that *do not* give rise to local extreme values are called **saddle points**.

For example, consider the hyperbolic paraboloid 

$$
z = f(x,y) = y^2-x^2
$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/ce/cea092da684db6b055c78369fcb987c3577a027ef0d8f03d598e115e85775ff5.png)

$$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60d15795-6c7a-5ec9-806d-625f5d8c5c85" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4264 :tutorial/title "Saddle Points"} {:db/id 17592186125487 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124570 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124379 :question/id #uuid "c6938151-ab77-5288-ba08-156dc942ddec" :question/math-academy-id "e-7030"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "40d58ee6-1121-5ddc-a96f-1a7fa7a193dd" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124821} {:db/id 17592186124822} {:db/id 17592186284418} {:db/id 17592186284419} {:db/id 17592186284423} {:db/id 17592186284424} {:db/id 17592186367881} {:db/id 17592186367888} {:db/id 17592186434754} {:db/id 17592186434755} {:db/id 17592186434759} {:db/id 17592186434764}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Local Extrema Using Sylvester's Criterion"} :step/id #uuid "98e2abbe-ffee-53fc-af20-297624f9d77a" :step/math-academy-id 25918} {:db/id 17592186125625 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124646 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124209 :question/id #uuid "137818ca-6c48-5ae1-8788-2015f7890ad5" :question/math-academy-id "e-12460"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3ee9cbe8-ad40-5155-b42d-1802f36adf27" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048164}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124811} {:db/id 17592186124812} {:db/id 17592186284436} {:db/id 17592186284450} {:db/id 17592186398583} {:db/id 17592186401426} {:db/id 17592186433377} {:db/id 17592186433378} {:db/id 17592186433379} {:db/id 17592186433380} {:db/id 17592186434758} {:db/id 17592186434762}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Global Extrema of a Multivariable Function"} :step/id #uuid "1bf38d19-ac54-50d2-9456-e7e1e26fc0a6" :step/math-academy-id 44845 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125628}} {:db/id 17592186125628 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125873 :tutorial/content "Now, recall the definition of local extrema for single-variable functions:

- A function $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x$-values in a neighborhood of $a.$

- A function $f(x)$ has a local maximum at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x$-values in a neighborhood of $a.$

On the function's graph, a local minimum is the lowest point of a valley, and a local maximum is the highest point of a peak.

![](images/ba/ba5be082363bd963514baa6b1a777f02098d53a3b0a80ddc2fad231e4669ebd7.png)

We can generalize the concept of local extrema to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ as follows:

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a local minimum at the point $\mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x}$ in a neighborhood of $\mathbf{a}.$

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a local maximum at the point $\mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x}$ in a neighborhood of $\mathbf{a}.$

In particular, for a function $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R},$ local minima and maxima are the lowest points in valleys and highest points in peaks, respectively, in the graph $z=f(x,y)$ of the function.

![](images/74/74d04165fd3bd5cd24ae82351bbf840e7d549b272c3deea16671dbfcd40bc75a.png)

For the points $A$ and $B,$ we can take neighborhoods of the $(x,y)$-values at these points such that $A$ and $B$ are the lowest points on the graph in these neighborhoods. Hence, they are local minima.

Similarly, for the points $C$ and $D,$ we can take neighborhoods of the $(x,y)$-values at these points such that $C$ and $D$ are the highest points on the graph in these neighborhoods. Hence, they are local maxima.

**Note**: For the point $E,$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f(x_E,y_E) = f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ or $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$, the point $E$ satisfies the conditions for a local minimum *and* a local maximum.

Finally, the points $F$ and $G$ are neither local minima nor local maxima. Notice that any neighborhood of $F$ will contain both points that lie higher than $F$ and lower than $F$ on the graph (similarly, for the point $G$)." :tutorial/id #uuid "fc6789c5-925e-54f4-9a5a-bfb179e77937" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7752 :tutorial/title "Local Extrema of a Multivariable Function"} :step/id #uuid "086acac3-3967-5f92-bf6e-ae6524a36328" :step/math-academy-id 44870 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125626}} {:db/id 17592186125626 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124647 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124210 :question/id #uuid "976e4ec4-93f9-57a4-9f2b-2116e09fed22" :question/math-academy-id "e-12461"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f0fb118f-c1cc-51fd-a8cc-c29cf705acfe" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050033}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124813} {:db/id 17592186124814} {:db/id 17592186235544} {:db/id 17592186284447} {:db/id 17592186284448} {:db/id 17592186284449} {:db/id 17592186401439} {:db/id 17592186434756} {:db/id 17592186434757} {:db/id 17592186434761} {:db/id 17592186434763} {:db/id 17592186434765} {:db/id 17592186445198}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Local Extrema of a Multivariable Function"} :step/id #uuid "4b1acac2-a584-5026-9cb7-d5e4ae42f3ee" :step/math-academy-id 44846 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125486}} {:db/id 17592186125873 :tutorial/content "Now, recall the definition of local extrema for single-variable functions:

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global minimum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global maximum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

On the function's graph, the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points, respectively.

![](images/63/633526565293f480a6a5fc45b87a70d38e946ae0f72a925f0074776e201a43a4.png)

We can generalize this concept to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global minimum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global minimum** of the function, the smallest value the function attains on its domain.

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global maximum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global maximum** of the function, the largest value the function attains on its domain.

In particular, for a function $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R},$ the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points on the graph $z=f(x,y),$ respectively.

![](images/de/de4cfc96fdce210430291999e5997f4a0c39ed1fbe63c3848b61508ca3f04114.png)

For the function shown above:

- The minimum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = -2,$ so the global minimum is $-2,$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,-1).$ Therefore the global minimum point is $(1,-1,-2).$

- Similarly, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = 2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,1).$ Therefore the global maximum point is $(1,1,2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c71de7-b70c-5b7f-a566-143fd897ff59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125885 :tutorial/content "To summarize, the point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a stationary point of the function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ if $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T,$ and we can classify $\mathbf{a}$ as follows:

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a local minimum

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a local maximum

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point" :tutorial/id #uuid "ab23ca4b-1bff-5c96-a4d2-62b72b8adff2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7852 :tutorial/title "A Summary of Key Results"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186445202} :activity/id #uuid "632f0c8c-4357-5396-aad3-4401d3471d8c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049676 :topic/id #uuid "0a177390-6525-5d0c-8721-f7f75db39408" :topic/math-academy-id 1945} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186445199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186367874 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "99f22169-b8a2-5fb3-aca1-3e5599415ad8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "local maximum" :db/id 17592186367876} {:answer/id #uuid "abbaa7f2-5259-5b5a-bebd-07f255b181e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "inconclusive" :db/id 17592186367877} {:answer/id #uuid "f674340e-9bc4-5748-9997-f0404db95ca2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "not a critical point" :db/id 17592186367878} {:answer/id #uuid "383240c1-34bf-5387-adaf-b9355e4cf27e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "local minimum" :db/id 17592186367879} {:answer/id #uuid "0e483432-9f14-537e-b0dd-61a175cc1645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "saddle point" :db/id 17592186367880}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367876} :answer-field/id #uuid "be669623-0526-55a8-9e58-06217378cfec" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367875}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1f0502ee-0a83-5915-919b-cb8a0333bfec" :question/math-academy-id "q-163775" :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{2}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 \\ 3 & -6\end{bmatrix}(x-a).
$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-9,$ what type of point is $a?$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-3<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-9<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. Therefore, $a$ is a local maximum of $f.$"} :step/id #uuid "40399da2-21fd-5f08-bac2-f30a1d0cf8b3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445203}} {:db/id 17592186445200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186445198 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "118339a7-669b-5081-8175-449ccce667f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The function does not have local maxima" :db/id 17592186445192} {:answer/id #uuid "80185868-d8d6-5a9a-9b8a-83d741afd936" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$B$ and $C$ only" :db/id 17592186445193} {:answer/id #uuid "b251a48a-e4be-5932-a217-f573cfba9f2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$C$ only" :db/id 17592186445194} {:answer/id #uuid "b9b3e9e9-2073-5961-8289-000100206e82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$B$ only" :db/id 17592186445195} {:answer/id #uuid "e2b33820-f35d-5434-abf3-958f348e4695" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$A$ only" :db/id 17592186445196}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186445196} :answer-field/id #uuid "261ceadd-9e63-5d86-9762-c5e81f0679da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186445197}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "da2e1b4b-fd99-52e9-91fa-fb0d43968219" :question/math-academy-id "q-164157" :question/problem "![](images/19/19f4f2d616fa648fcd4663be22b32ab18662fffa8e31f9bd44f0dd3b6da99208.png)

The graph of the function $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. Which of the points shown are local maximum points?" :question/worked-solution "A function $f(x,y)$ has a local maximum point at $(a,b)$ if $f(x,y)\le f(a,b)$ for all points $(x,y)$ in a neighborhood of $(a,b).$ 

In other words, we can take a neighborhood of $(x,y)$-values such that the point $(x,y,f(x,y))$ is the highest point on the graph in the neighborhood.

Such region exists for the point $A.$ Hence, $A$ is a local maximum point.

**Note**: For the point $A({x}_{A},{y}_{A},{z}_{A}),$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f({x}_{A},{y}_{A})=f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(x,y)\le f(a,b)$, the point $A$ does satisfy the conditions for a local maximum.

The graph $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. What are the global minimum points of the function?" :question/worked-solution "First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global minimum of a function is the smallest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global minimum.

$$
f(x)≈1+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 \\ 3 & -6\end{bmatrix}(x-a).
$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-9,$ what type of point is $a?$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-3<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-9<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. The graph $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. What are the global maximum points of the function?" :question/worked-solution "First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global maximum of a function is the largest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum.

- A global maximum point is a point $(x,y,z)$ where a function reaches a global maximum. There can be zero, one, or many global maximum points.

For our function, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y)=3.$ Therefore, the global maximum is $3.$ The function reaches this value when $(x,y)=(-2,1),$ so the global maximum point is $(-2,1,3).$

:question/math-academy-id "q-163722" :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{2}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈-12+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}A(x-a),
$$

where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=-2$ and $det(A)=-24$

- **II.** $A$ is positive-definite

- **III.** $a$ is a local minimum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, let's recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-2$ and

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}|=-24.
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-2<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}|=-24<0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite.

- Statement III is false. Since the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a saddle point of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} :step/id #uuid "647913e4-ab77-5ef3-a66f-ab77b352f8b2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520584}} {:db/id 17592186520570 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284422 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "40769601-5e6b-5811-8d87-d4e245a3b44b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "inconclusive" :db/id 17592186282244} {:answer/id #uuid "697f5a10-56de-5e96-8d49-0b219f74b52d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "not a critical point" :db/id 17592186282594} {:answer/id #uuid "8cc1225a-208e-5576-8fa1-8495783e27ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "saddle point" :db/id 17592186282909} {:answer/id #uuid "994080d1-474f-5f19-920a-c11b2301f486" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "local maximum" :db/id 17592186283021} {:answer/id #uuid "9a0fe6f7-98c5-5152-b74a-4001671d9b6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "local minimum" :db/id 17592186283032}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186283032} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebbb4b19-fdb5-5b6d-a6cf-ba581d730234" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284348}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "45b6a4ae-c84e-567c-b717-cd9dbeea1d7b" :question/math-academy-id "q-163785" :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{3}$ is given by

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-1<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-3<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. - if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that ${f}^{″}(a)$ has both negative and positive eigenvalues:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =1-\sqrt{5}<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =1+\sqrt{5}>0\end{aligned}

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-1<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-3<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "A function $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum point at $(a,b)$ if $f(x,y)\ge f(a,b)$ for all points $(x,y)$ in a neighborhood of $(a,b).$ 

In other words, we can take a neighborhood of $(x,y)$-values such that the point $(x,y,f(x,y))$ is the lowest point on the graph in the neighborhood.

Such regions exist for the points $B$ and $D.$ Hence, $B$ and $D$ are local minimum points.

**Note**: For the point $D({x}_{D},{y}_{D},{z}_{D}),$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f({x}_{D},{y}_{D})=f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(x,y)\ge f(a,b)$, the point $D$ does satisfy the conditions for a local minimum.

$$

$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1+\sqrt{26}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1-\sqrt{26},$ what type of point is $a?$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that ${f}^{″}(a)$ has both negative and positive eigenvalues:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-1+\sqrt{26}>0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-1-\sqrt{26}<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite. Therefore, $a$ is a saddle point of $f.$"} :step/id #uuid "90845892-a21e-5ed0-8f4d-4176220e88dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186554743}} {:db/id 17592186554721 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284424 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bf8f149-6cad-5a5c-9d26-11b86bcaa720" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465519} {:answer/id #uuid "6b04f584-4740-59cf-8497-f747191febb3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465520}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465520} :answer-field/id #uuid "ddfefddd-b168-5878-87f2-f8f0e1876a2e" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466603} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9f9329ab-4f40-5e23-86a5-bf4d0b285377" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465521} {:answer/id #uuid "5441ae78-27c1-5694-8618-d6f72b5ef496" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465522}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465522} :answer-field/id #uuid "d143db0c-e1c0-5daa-9470-d0193838ae88" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466604} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12620dec-4540-5bfc-a97c-4be11c2d223d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186465523} {:answer/id #uuid "13ec6254-73f7-5076-8506-15526b0e95bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186465524}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186465523} :answer-field/id #uuid "c993b7a5-1549-5886-b715-49e5a62df038" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186466605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "00b2158a-941e-5a2f-b68c-c230bee6df19" :question/math-academy-id "q-163791" :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{3}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈8+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}A(x-a),
$$

where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $det(A)=-19$
- **II.** $A$ is negative-definite
- **III.** $a$ is a local minimum of $f$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(11)-1(-3) \\  & =-19.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-2<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}|=7>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-19<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is negative-definite.

- Statement III is false. Since the matrix $A$ is negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a local maximum of $f.$

$$

where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -4 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Which of the following statements are true?

- **II.** $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite
- **III.** $a$ is a saddle point of $f$

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=3,$ but

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -4 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-4)\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(3)-1(-2)-4(7) \\  & =-17<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=3>0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|=5>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-17<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite.

- Statement III is true. Since the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a saddle point of $f.$

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum
