$$

Similarly, if we wanted to compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t},$ we would highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$

![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

Keeping $s$ fixed and differentiating $f$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "58d189b1-31fb-5b1b-bc4c-cff6be5e2f7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4958 :tutorial/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule With Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "2ffafece-1c0b-50f7-a3b1-e1b2d1bada36" :step/math-academy-id 30894 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167575}} {:db/id 17592186167575 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166749 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166587 :question/id #uuid "1491963b-fbd8-57fa-bdde-f2d6705fbb83" :question/math-academy-id "e-8258"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f26d941b-b4b4-591e-b7e0-ae4bbf81e94b" :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186529504} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167311} {:db/id 17592186167325} {:db/id 17592186284668} {:db/id 17592186284669} {:db/id 17592186323886} {:db/id 17592186360483} {:db/id 17592186360484} {:db/id 17592186378038} {:db/id 17592186385363} {:db/id 17592186385824} {:db/id 17592186437272} {:db/id 17592186479133} {:db/id 17592186529474} {:db/id 17592186529477} {:db/id 17592186529480} {:db/id 17592186529488} {:db/id 17592186529494}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "60b2ea1e-4b9a-5557-99ae-a83016e785a6" :step/math-academy-id 30863 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167579}} {:db/id 17592186167579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168063 :tutorial/content "We can generalize the chain rule to a multivariable function containing an arbitrary number of intermediate and independent variables.

Consider the multivariable function 

$$
f = f(x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_m)
$$

with $m$ independent variables and, for each $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\},$ the variable 

$$
x_i = g_i(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n)
$$

is a differentiable function of $n$ independent variables. Then,

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t_j} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial t_j} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial t_j} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_m}{\partial t_j}
$$

for $j \in \{1,2,\ldots, n\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ba7d2a4-05a6-5e62-8035-2610239633c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4959 :tutorial/title "The Generalized Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "9731a04f-c2d1-5342-b940-0313b71ca1eb" :step/math-academy-id 30895 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167576}} {:db/id 17592186167576 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166750 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166588 :question/id #uuid "e535fe44-a3cb-5c11-831c-118b90582c0d" :question/math-academy-id "e-8259"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71c243ca-5d46-58d2-bd16-28075c04d2db" :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186546131} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167328} {:db/id 17592186167329} {:db/id 17592186284670} {:db/id 17592186323885} {:db/id 17592186360507} {:db/id 17592186360508} {:db/id 17592186360509} {:db/id 17592186360510} {:db/id 17592186360511} {:db/id 17592186383614} {:db/id 17592186385370} {:db/id 17592186420996} {:db/id 17592186546100} {:db/id 17592186546109} {:db/id 17592186546113} {:db/id 17592186546116} {:db/id 17592186546118}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "26ddca41-ae16-5395-ae11-41c4d70303c6" :step/math-academy-id 30864} {:db/id 17592186168061 :tutorial/content "The chain rule for single variable functions $f=f(x)$ and $x=x(t)$ states that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.
$$

Let's now suppose that $f = f(x,y),$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t)$ are single-variable functions. How do we find $\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d t}$ in this case?

The functions $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are known as **intermediate variables.** They are independent variables for the function $f(x,y),$ but are themselves dependent on the variable $t.$

One way to consider how $f(x,y)$ depends on $t$ is to draw a tree diagram.

Starting with $f(x,y),$ we draw a branch for each intermediate variable. Then, we draw a branch for both $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ which are both dependent on the variable $t.$

![](images/cd/cdc47e038ecaba62ae612a0ac0bc07067af232353fc4fc169bf4be57b3abbd1f.png)

We then label each branch with the derivative describing how the function changes due to a change in the variable. 

![](images/ec/ece6012e358b5b6920395df88acd8d7037a7b15bed1add1220365ba72bd24cbd.png)

Then, traversing each branch, we compute the product of the derivatives along each branch and place the result at the end of the branch.

![](images/f0/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

Finally, to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t},$ we sum the results for each branch:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t}
 = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

This result is called the **multivariable chain rule**." :tutorial/id #uuid "80ad8a26-7d43-52d6-b0ba-e1d04283e5ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4957 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186168062 :tutorial/content "How do we apply the multivariable chain rule if the intermediate variables are also dependent on two variables? 

For example, suppose we have

$$
f = f(x,y), \qquad x=g(s,t), \qquad y=h(s,t).
$$

How do we compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s}?$ 

First, let's construct a tree diagram.

![](images/ca/ca524eda2e6be3354fcb72bed52fcaf22257073c3228d74850f8226f9ef0af6f.png)

Now, since we're interested in $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s},$ we highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $s:$

![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

If we keep $t$ fixed and differentiate $f$ with respect to $s,$ then according to the chain rule for two intermediate variables and one independent variable, we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s}.
$$

Similarly, if we wanted to compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t},$ we would highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$

![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

Keeping $s$ fixed and differentiating $f$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "58d189b1-31fb-5b1b-bc4c-cff6be5e2f7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4958 :tutorial/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule With Two Independent Variables"} {:db/id 17592186168063 :tutorial/content "We can generalize the chain rule to a multivariable function containing an arbitrary number of intermediate and independent variables.

Consider the multivariable function 

$$
f = f(x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_m)
$$

with $m$ independent variables and, for each $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\},$ the variable 

$$
x_i = g_i(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n)
$$

is a differentiable function of $n$ independent variables. Then,

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t_j} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial t_j} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial t_j} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_m}{\partial t_j}
$$

for $j \in \{1,2,\ldots, n\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ba7d2a4-05a6-5e62-8035-2610239633c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4959 :tutorial/title "The Generalized Multivariable Chain Rule"} {:db/id 17592186168088 :tutorial/content "There is a special case of the multivariable chain rule when $f=f(x,y)$ and $y=g(x).$ 

Notice that $x$ is an independent variable here. Therefore, the chain rule becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}}_{⏟}}_{1}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "44effd03-02e7-5eb1-8732-ee1522afa147" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5184 :tutorial/title "A Special Case of the Multivariable Chain Rule"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186420998} :activity/id #uuid "844676a2-0a90-5f03-a7c1-22515b371e49" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050031 :topic/id #uuid "27615ef6-ec0e-5e91-b58b-24b70dc01a09" :topic/math-academy-id 3173} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186420997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167325 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a19a158-cb30-5c9e-9cf9-891ab114ad36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(2t-1)" :db/id 17592186355012} {:answer/id #uuid "392f1f1c-1dad-5e72-b1e4-40cf201a767c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}t(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355179} {:answer/id #uuid "869f5f73-0c65-5003-ade6-8eeef3e8b4ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355855} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f0fe58-16c4-5d79-ab11-4893e9ff089a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(s-1)" :db/id 17592186356369} {:answer/id #uuid "fa6ace28-41b6-5a2e-8b64-9dee698d22fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(t-1)" :db/id 17592186356853}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356853} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314b903-87e4-5c8c-a8db-703d520d008b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e1e3cf4a-155f-587d-ba03-cc737759407e" :question/math-academy-id "q-94448" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-4y,$ where $x=2st$ and $y={s}^{2}t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2cf7698e-82a3-5979-93cb-d2edffbb99d7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421000}} {:db/id 17592186420998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323885 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a9a8991-24fd-50f9-8941-a329e3133c45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+10{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186321230} {:answer/id #uuid "84b790fb-dce2-5ea5-9fbd-fb66967b78c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-20s\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322195} {:answer/id #uuid "bb1f027a-f67b-5d1f-b407-9ee3b85b3667" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322598} {:answer/id #uuid "c8bfc905-fde6-54a5-83ad-c5fa1e325d7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322709} {:answer/id #uuid "f675ee7a-8c5d-5a9a-90cb-d0e4dd971fe3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-15s\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186323079}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322709} :answer-field/id #uuid "af1de9ae-38d9-5d66-a275-9fc76c319cbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323509}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bd5b5db6-0961-5b1c-8f50-24c2f4348bc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-37132" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y-5yz,$ where $x=st,$ $y={s}^{3}$ and $z=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6a9db776-142d-5ace-9b62-834d4e4b6a63" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421001}} {:db/id 17592186420999 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284667 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "021a846a-8825-55bf-a7b3-1dc5c5c5ff19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186281709} {:answer/id #uuid "49b2d0a3-8640-5928-a7d2-f8a14102a68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))" :db/id 17592186282314} {:answer/id #uuid "e8a1e1c7-9e8a-5f17-9500-4d7507d44b3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283715} {:answer/id #uuid "efd819c9-60d2-5826-9266-3dba4a49aaec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283779} {:answer/id #uuid "f5de75cd-c44e-5baf-9f07-d98f3333edab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186283839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282314} :answer-field/id #uuid "d658fcd0-7d37-5a87-a5b6-42706ffef583" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284307}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cdba7da9-8893-51f6-a38d-eccc847b176c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170670" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ and $y={x}^{2}+1,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6ef0c797-03b2-58eb-8a37-83236f476fe8"} {:db/id 17592186421000 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360569 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4be18679-efe0-59e6-80ac-db92f8d96a8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186358407} {:answer/id #uuid "4f9edd72-2523-57c6-9665-681f1ed475c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186358439} {:answer/id #uuid "9bcdf56c-f98e-5632-8b37-69db930425d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186359116} {:answer/id #uuid "9f4b3c97-4572-526c-8afd-d0a1d5757af5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186359141} {:answer/id #uuid "b33efd16-e5a4-5396-8988-6df4afae8ae5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186359315}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186358407} :answer-field/id #uuid "1f643ac2-8342-50cb-9136-e026a1d69059" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360047}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cfb1f74a-0323-5d9e-a2f6-877356ed98f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-95118" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+yx$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+{c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}st+{c}_{3}s{t}^{4},

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "926bef20-92d0-5cd4-928e-9a8dd40763b1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420997}}] :activity/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186420989} {:db/id 17592186420998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323885 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a9a8991-24fd-50f9-8941-a329e3133c45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+10{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186321230} {:answer/id #uuid "84b790fb-dce2-5ea5-9fbd-fb66967b78c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-20s\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322195} {:answer/id #uuid "bb1f027a-f67b-5d1f-b407-9ee3b85b3667" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322598} {:answer/id #uuid "c8bfc905-fde6-54a5-83ad-c5fa1e325d7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322709} {:answer/id #uuid "f675ee7a-8c5d-5a9a-90cb-d0e4dd971fe3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-15s\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186323079}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322709} :answer-field/id #uuid "af1de9ae-38d9-5d66-a275-9fc76c319cbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323509}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bd5b5db6-0961-5b1c-8f50-24c2f4348bc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-37132" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y-5yz,$ where $x=st,$ $y={s}^{3}$ and $z=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6a9db776-142d-5ace-9b62-834d4e4b6a63" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421001}} {:db/id 17592186420997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167325 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a19a158-cb30-5c9e-9cf9-891ab114ad36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(2t-1)" :db/id 17592186355012} {:answer/id #uuid "392f1f1c-1dad-5e72-b1e4-40cf201a767c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}t(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355179} {:answer/id #uuid "869f5f73-0c65-5003-ade6-8eeef3e8b4ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355855} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f0fe58-16c4-5d79-ab11-4893e9ff089a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(s-1)" :db/id 17592186356369} {:answer/id #uuid "fa6ace28-41b6-5a2e-8b64-9dee698d22fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(t-1)" :db/id 17592186356853}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356853} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314b903-87e4-5c8c-a8db-703d520d008b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e1e3cf4a-155f-587d-ba03-cc737759407e" :question/math-academy-id "q-94448" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-4y,$ where $x=2st$ and $y={s}^{2}t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "926bef20-92d0-5cd4-928e-9a8dd40763b1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420997}} {:db/id 17592186420999 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284667 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "021a846a-8825-55bf-a7b3-1dc5c5c5ff19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186281709} {:answer/id #uuid "49b2d0a3-8640-5928-a7d2-f8a14102a68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))" :db/id 17592186282314} {:answer/id #uuid "e8a1e1c7-9e8a-5f17-9500-4d7507d44b3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283715} {:answer/id #uuid "efd819c9-60d2-5826-9266-3dba4a49aaec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283779} {:answer/id #uuid "f5de75cd-c44e-5baf-9f07-d98f3333edab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186283839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282314} :answer-field/id #uuid "d658fcd0-7d37-5a87-a5b6-42706ffef583" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284307}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cdba7da9-8893-51f6-a38d-eccc847b176c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170670" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ and $y={x}^{2}+1,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

"q-94749" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)=xy,$ where $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(st)$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(st).$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(st))(s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st))+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(st))(-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st)) \\  & =s{cos}^{2}⁡(st)-s{sin}^{2}⁡(st) \\  & =s({cos}^{2}⁡(st)-{sin}^{2}⁡(st)) \\  & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(2st).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "03f2df0e-7127-5bf6-a3cb-55f1736639ac" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515646}} {:db/id 17592186515646 :step/content {:db/id 17592186479104 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4d5ecadd-1d99-51f3-b3ee-0d0a52a7e504" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2{e}^{2x}}{x+{e}^{2x}}" :db/id 17592186478669} {:answer/id #uuid "7eececa3-aed5-56bc-8acd-83a7d9f52ce0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{1+2{e}^{2x}}" :db/id 17592186478748} {:answer/id #uuid "c04864f4-8e0e-5d9d-8763-0a9d20cfc1c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1+{e}^{2x}}{x+{e}^{2x}}" :db/id 17592186478870} {:answer/id #uuid "c22286df-0bd2-569b-80cb-dd78460f6e01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2x}}{x+{e}^{2x}}" :db/id 17592186478871} {:answer/id #uuid "fd87021b-423b-576b-b08a-47b84980a27a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1+2{e}^{2x}}{x+{e}^{2x}}" :db/id 17592186478956}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186478956} :answer-field/id #uuid "3f1b30ab-e87a-541b-926a-088f06d1391d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186478982}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "889d0bfa-8294-56c7-a3ce-0b0d572aff69" :question/math-academy-id "q-95120" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$ and $y={e}^{2x},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x+{e}^{2x}}+\frac{1}{x+{e}^{2x}}\cdot 2{e}^{2x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+{e}^{2x}}+\frac{2{e}^{2x}}{x+{e}^{2x}} \\  & =\frac{1+2{e}^{2x}}{x+{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3c096bca-7b75-5ffa-8b01-bdd0cb2ca5b9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186515674}} {:db/id 17592186515674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186383614 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8172957c-8ded-58d3-9a23-800391f6abc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{s}" :db/id 17592186383616} {:answer/id #uuid "65fc28e8-01f1-5779-81a2-95006d854621" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{s}-2t" :db/id 17592186383617} {:answer/id #uuid "78f76e21-a29b-5ac4-bef0-5e96cc36b301" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{e}^{s}-2" :db/id 17592186383618} {:answer/id #uuid "1650585c-4f5b-5c09-98dc-1b8f36155d98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{s}+2+t" :db/id 17592186383619} {:answer/id #uuid "9d243851-27bb-5ff4-9d66-8de5b61c5110" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{e}^{s}+t" :db/id 17592186383620}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186383618} :answer-field/id #uuid "a31244f4-c1a2-50a4-adcb-bc5510fae670" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186383615}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "04777d40-e9e1-5da3-94ee-34ffd4874f77" :question/math-academy-id "q-170674" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)=z-x-y,$ where $x={e}^{s}+t,$ $y=s+1$ and $z=1-t-s.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(-1)\cdot {e}^{s}+(-1)\cdot 1+(1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-{e}^{s}-2.\end{aligned}

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(t-s)(2st)=4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =(t-s)^{2}={t}^{2}-2st+{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =3, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)\cdot 3+(4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t)\cdot 1+({t}^{2}-2st+{s}^{2})\cdot 2s \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+4s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t+2s{t}^{2}-4{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{3} \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t+6s{t}^{2}-8{s}^{2}t+2{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=6,$ ${c}_{2}=-8$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=6+(-8)+2=0.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(-1)\cdot {e}^{s}+(-1)\cdot 1+(1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-{e}^{s}-2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a1ec6cd0-639d-5c32-a34b-e1f726d9e5e0"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8172957c-8ded-58d3-9a23-800391f6abc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}=\frac{2}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{cot}⁡t-\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1d1473e6-3651-50ed-9ec9-88f004e468cd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519623}} {:db/id 17592186519619 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360556 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b80e388-89f0-55d3-9647-29eb1e7d21a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186357986} {:answer/id #uuid "2931a144-34bf-5b91-9fd0-2c8561636d73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡2s+{csc}^{2}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186358129} {:answer/id #uuid "5f982da7-fadd-5a18-83b3-b5af485d42fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cot}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186358586} {:answer/id #uuid "981660b8-6d8e-5d6b-a353-cc9e60ac0aac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{tan}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186359084} {:answer/id #uuid "d2b01e60-3c8a-5b80-ab36-ad8a68a5308f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{sec}^{2}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186359593}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186357986} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce0a50c8-6fe1-52e2-992d-16da1ca6ce29" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360348}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f22cdf5c-424c-5c09-91c4-a4b6bd7748c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-95084" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y},x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2s$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/7e/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{2xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot 1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}

$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =s{e}^{\sqrt{s}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1f2d63e2-db91-599f-ba79-b154350da4c1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186519639}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b80e388-89f0-55d3-9647-29eb1e7d21a2" :answer/type {:db/id \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1cab00d5-4da8-576c-bf80-814a66279e8a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186524081}} {:db/id 17592186524052 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360571 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06a85a62-20c8-53ea-9891-50994f57bf9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4{x}^{2}(x-6)}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186357811} {:answer/id #uuid "31bd0322-e103-58db-ab4e-d490d4079dbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}(3{x}^{2}-1)}{(x+1)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186358194} {:answer/id #uuid "870209e6-e356-5edd-a169-1a95385cbde9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(3x+4)}{(x+1)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186358933} {:answer/id #uuid "c0ec2678-1f3d-53f9-9edd-d1c6fda28115" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(4x-3)}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186359444} {:answer/id #uuid "d1925cff-23b1-5f65-a480-35f2ce80acbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186359584}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359584} :answer-field/id #uuid "a27a35b5-3297-5a09-b127-d1d744a50e89" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360275}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f411889e-b3c1-5aed-8247-b760065e6e98" :question/math-academy-id "q-95122" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x+1}$ and $y={x}^{3},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3a017487-80b3-5b03-a1d5-2934bfa2d036"} {:db/id 17592186524081 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360555 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "46f944b8-e799-5036-80f1-5ba5c1a7411f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186358364} {:answer/id #uuid "82479d60-5437-50e5-882f-1cefac414e6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186358893} {:answer/id #uuid "f1724fb0-eb83-58dc-8a3f-92689c7862c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{ln}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186359901} {:answer/id #uuid "fe84e3ca-9757-54b8-a1da-085a92705bae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186359990} {:answer/id #uuid "fede68b1-836b-57e9-a83f-57bb56eb0c3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s" :db/id 17592186359994}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186358893} :answer-field/id #uuid "ef608987-b651-5ccb-b9c8-ffdc510994e1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360424}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b0e7724b-5745-517d-9a70-23d66bdba953" :question/math-academy-id "q-95081" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=y+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x=s$ and $y=2s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/7e/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9e72f9a3-b2cc-52fb-b449-d5acf347acc1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186524041}} {:db/id 17592186524107 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360570 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23dbcf33-c576-54cf-8c07-43b62cf69983" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1+4{x}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{x})" :db/id 17592186358069} {:answer/id #uuid "558df00d-6a5e-5bb3-bb8a-e8288e5b1e90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1-4{x}^{3}}{x})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{2}})" :db/id 17592186358497} {:answer/id #uuid "67861fb7-92d5-5f5e-8f74-f8ff3c7f315c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1-3{x}^{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{x}^{2}})" :db/id 17592186358655} {:answer/id #uuid "70539894-ff4f-5b7d-809c-ae8c476c88fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x})" :db/id 17592186358729} {:answer/id #uuid "da024232-5563-5f22-a044-1622a067232a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2{x}^{2}+1}{x})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x})" :db/id 17592186359659}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186358729} :answer-field/id #uuid "f550e8b8-0dda-5ff3-ba5c-bfed41503899" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360429}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5f396a56-19fc-58e7-855c-d3a310fbb9ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-95119" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y)$ and $y=\frac{1}{x},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1cab00d5-4da8-576c-bf80-814a66279e8a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186524081}} {:db/id 17592186524041 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360569 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4be18679-efe0-59e6-80ac-db92f8d96a8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186358407} {:answer/id #uuid "4f9edd72-2523-57c6-9665-681f1ed475c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186358439} {:answer/id #uuid "9bcdf56c-f98e-5632-8b37-69db930425d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x" :db/id 17592186359116} {:answer/id #uuid "9f4b3c97-4572-526c-8afd-d0a1d5757af5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186359141} {:answer/id #uuid "b33efd16-e5a4-5396-8988-6df4afae8ae5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡x" :db/id 17592186359315}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186358407} :answer-field/id #uuid "1f643ac2-8342-50cb-9136-e026a1d69059" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360047}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cfb1f74a-0323-5d9e-a2f6-877356ed98f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-95118" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+yx$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/7e/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9e72f9a3-b2cc-52fb-b449-d5acf347acc1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186524041}} {:db/id 17592186524052 :step/content {:db/id 17592186360571 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06a85a62-20c8-53ea-9891-50994f57bf9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4{x}^{2}(x-6)}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186357811} {:answer/id #uuid "31bd0322-e103-58db-ab4e-d490d4079dbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}(3{x}^{2}-1)}{(x+1)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186358194} {:answer/id #uuid "870209e6-e356-5edd-a169-1a95385cbde9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(3x+4)}{(x+1)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186358933} {:answer/id #uuid "c0ec2678-1f3d-53f9-9edd-d1c6fda28115" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x(4x-3)}{x+1}" :db/id 17592186359444} {:answer/id #uuid "d1925cff-23b1-5f65-a480-35f2ce80acbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186359584}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186359584} :answer-field/id #uuid "a27a35b5-3297-5a09-b127-d1d744a50e89" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186360275}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f411889e-b3c1-5aed-8247-b760065e6e98" :question/math-academy-id "q-95122" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x+1}$ and $y={x}^{3},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

"4d32e47e-9f37-5a31-95c8-7aa1fca70d66" :topic/math-academy-id 4132} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199250 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199451 :tutorial/content "Suppose that 

$$
\mathbf T: (u,v) \to \left(x(u,v),y(u,v)\right)
$$

is a $C^1$ transformation that has no critical points (i.e., it is invertible) inside some region $\Delta\subset \mathbb R^2,$ and that $\mathbf T(\Delta) = D,$ as shown below.

![](images/66/668b8a0dae060c7929b92c6abe3601b0ede0b8444d92f33f4a8b5627410a4447.png)

 

We've already seen how the area of a non-trivial region $D$ can be computed using the change of variables formula:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

We can extend this formula to compute the integral of a function $f(x,y)$ over $D,$ as follows:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \:  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

Note the similarity with the change of variables formula for the integral of a single-variable function $f(x)$ over $D = (a,b){:}$

$$
\int\limits_D f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} f(x(u))\,\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u
$$

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

We can extend this formula to compute the integral of a function $f(x,y)$ over $D,$ as follows:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \:  \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

$$
\int\limits_D f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} f(x(u))\,\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u
$$

"q-160896" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,0),$ $(2,-1),$ $(2,2),$ and $(1,3).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x-1,\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(2(1)-1,1+0) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-1) & =(2(2)-1,2+(-1)) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,2) & =(2(2)-1,2+2) \\  & =(3,4) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,3) & =(2(1)-1,1+3) \\  & =(1,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 4\}
$$

![](images/1d/1d5943d2cf79e7c77f6db3e939242d7e31068f46506fa618abd24b6ac813d32a.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{v}^{2}\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{1}^{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 21\cdot 4\,\text{d}v \\  & =42.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1e5d6fdb-4349-5a22-9a20-57fac957a381" :step/next {:db/id 17592186501295}} {:db/id 17592186501274 :step/content {:db/id 17592186501235 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c949071-0d3c-54bb-9dc4-96b0d8539778" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186500621} {:answer/id #uuid "610bdf54-043a-5740-ad3a-0dec8d2b57b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{4}-1" :db/id 17592186500665} {:answer/id #uuid "663bf8f7-c948-5768-ae58-7d976d853146" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{4}" :db/id 17592186500680} {:answer/id #uuid "cee0c053-9570-5242-9c89-c00687d42bb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186500911} {:answer/id #uuid "dde36f82-c9e7-56b6-95a2-ab881de27e91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4({e}^{2}-1)" :db/id 17592186500939}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186500939} :answer-field/id #uuid "bb9e74ba-160b-54c7-b340-b16d836e9f06" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501105}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ea3ea5b4-3a71-55fd-af96-eb417a578734" :question/math-academy-id "q-160895" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

$$

$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=(x-y){e}^{x+y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x-y,\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(0,0) & =(0-0,0+0) \\  & =(0,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-2) & =(2-(-2),2+(-2)) \\  & =(4,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,-1) & =(3-(-1),3+(-1)) \\  & =(4,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,1) & =(1-1,1+1) \\  & =(0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,0\le v\le 2\}
$$

![](images/0b/0b23c6463447aa1fb64bdeeca689a40711f8dad59b348bb7943c2b9d2de7e8fc.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x-y){e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{e}^{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{e}^{v}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4}u{e}^{v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{4}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot [{e}^{v}]_{0}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{0}^{4}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({e}^{2}-1)\cdot 8 \\  & =4({e}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{y-2x}{y+2x}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y-2x\le 2,\,2\le y+2x\le 6\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le y-2x\le 2,\,2\le y+2x\le 6,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=y-2x\,\text{and}\,v=y+2x.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,2\le v\le 6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ \text{ }\text{ }\text{ }2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{4}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y-2x}{y+2x}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}|-\frac{1}{4}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u[{\int }_{2}^{6}\frac{1}{v}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u[\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|]_{2}^{6}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u(\operatorname{ln}⁡6-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3\,du \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b7040396-b7ee-5a68-99f5-cbdc7c619831"} {:db/id 17592186501290 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495100 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "36ad6cac-d25a-50df-a71c-ff5530463782" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-4\pi " :db/id 17592186494431} {:answer/id #uuid "377131c4-9276-5492-90f4-5fe9f9ea094b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2\pi }" :db/id 17592186494433} {:answer/id #uuid "389c158d-eca4-5138-ade2-702a2174ac43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(2\pi -1)" :db/id 17592186494436} {:answer/id #uuid "76f8296f-42f1-5d17-a5c6-7274b014898c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{12}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186494571} {:answer/id #uuid "adfbcfe0-1ed2-552d-9eab-c92cbe93246a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{6\pi }" :db/id 17592186494723}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494571} :answer-field/id #uuid "caaee621-928c-5865-8689-d0a675bcc7ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495012}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "75903bf3-d1b7-5813-a3cf-49663583fcbd" :question/math-academy-id "q-160915" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

$$

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "c69702c1-10b7-5ba2-9e9f-d73b85226694" :step/next {:db/id 17592186501286}} {:db/id 17592186501295 :step/content {:db/id 17592186493956 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b6b5fe5-29d1-5793-a274-fa3b5699e913" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3({e}^{-1/2}-{e}^{-2})\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186493410} {:answer/id #uuid "17dcff5e-6574-5e2e-be4c-22c67c1a31d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{8}" :db/id 17592186493432} {:answer/id #uuid "702b0bc2-ac10-5437-9f18-9fa877532a9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-1}-{e}^{-2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186493554} {:answer/id #uuid "857734df-e10d-5568-a049-4e87b8b5c0d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186493601} {:answer/id #uuid "e162164d-9035-55fa-9f1c-b47ea0bae241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "({e}^{2}-e)\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186493747}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493410} :answer-field/id #uuid "15ea503e-c96f-567a-8f89-cf26cc3e1193" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493808}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c5c02db8-6f5e-5ac6-a24e-9e9016b1082e" :question/math-academy-id "q-160899" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=\frac{y}{x}$ and $v=xy,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}{e}^{-xy/2}\,dx\,dy,

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{x}{4}\le y\le 2x,\,1\le xy\le 4\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{x},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{(-\frac{2y}{x})}=-\frac{1}{2u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{-xy/2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{-v/2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{-v/2}\cdot |-\frac{1}{2u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1/4}^{2}\frac{{e}^{-v/2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[{\int }_{1/4}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1/4}^{2}]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{1}{4}]\,du \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}\,du \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}\cdot {[-2{e}^{-v/2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot ({e}^{-2}-{e}^{-1/2}) \\  & =3({e}^{-1/2}-{e}^{-2})\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
